questions.memo: Diamonds and gold → mining capital → British imperialism → the South African War (1899–1902) → the Union of 1910. One connected chain.

questions.question: Place these events in chronological order — earliest first.

items.text: Diamonds discovered at Kimberley (1860s)
Gold discovered on the Witwatersrand (1886)
The South African (Anglo-Boer) War (1899–1902)
The Union of South Africa is formed (1910)

questions.memo: Kimberley diamonds (1860s) → Witwatersrand gold (1886) → the war (1899–1902) → the Union (1910). The minerals came first and set everything else in motion.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show this writer justifying British control as a noble mission rather than a grab for mineral wealth.
questions.source_text: It is the destiny of the British race to bring order, progress and Christian civilisation to these territories, and the great wealth beneath the soil is but a happy means to that higher end.
questions.task: Tap the phrases that disguise the hunt for wealth as a civilising mission.

targets.phrase: destiny of the British race
targets.reason: Claims a racial right to rule

targets.phrase: order, progress and Christian civilisation
targets.reason: Frames conquest as a gift rather than a grab

targets.phrase: a happy means to that higher end
targets.reason: Pretends mineral wealth is a side benefit, not the goal

questions.memo: 'Destiny of the British race', a mission of 'civilisation', wealth as a mere 'happy means' — all dress up a hard scramble for diamonds and gold as a noble duty.

questions.question: The treaty that ended the South African War in 1902 was the Treaty of:
questions.memo: The Treaty of Vereeniging (31 May 1902) ended the war and began the cooperation between British and Afrikaner whites that led to the Union of 1910.

questions.question: Sort each group by whether it was INCLUDED in or EXCLUDED from political power in the Union of 1910.

items.text: British English-speaking whites
Afrikaner whites
The African majority
Indian South Africans
Coloured South Africans (largely)
White mine owners and politicians

questions.memo: The Union gave power to whites (British and Afrikaner) and excluded the African majority, along with Indian and (largely) Coloured South Africans. The new state was built on racial exclusion.

questions.question: What does it tell us that former British and Boer enemies cooperated to form the Union just eight years after fighting a war?
options: White unity was built on a shared interest in ruling over the black majority
They had forgotten the war completely
Africans had asked them to unite
The war had never really happened
questions.expected: White unity was built on a shared interest in ruling over the black majority
questions.memo: Despite their bitter war, white British and Afrikaners found common ground in maintaining white control over the African majority — that shared racial interest underpinned the Union.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'In South Africa, the mineral revolution and politics were one story, not two.'
questions.thesis: In South Africa, the mineral revolution and politics were one story, not two.

pool.text: Control of mineral wealth drove British imperialism and the conquest of African polities
The hunger for gold helped trigger the South African War of 1899–1902
The Union of 1910 secured white political control over the labour and land the mines needed
Gold is a shiny yellow metal
Kimberley is in the Northern Cape
The mineral revolution also brought new technology and railways

questions.memo: Minerals drove imperialism (e1), helped cause the war (e2), and shaped the political settlement of 1910 (e3). e6 is true but a side point — the economic and political stories were tightly linked.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why the Union of 1910 is described as exclusionary.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why the Union of 1910 is described as exclusionary.

options.text: The Union united white South Africans while shutting out the African majority
The Union gave equal rights to everyone
The Union had no effect on political rights
British and Afrikaner whites held political power while over 80% of the population was denied citizenship rights
The Union was formed in 1910
South Africa has gold and diamonds
By building the state on white unity over the black majority, the Union entrenched racial exclusion in South Africa's foundations
The exclusion made no difference to anyone
Everyone was happy with the arrangement

questions.memo: Claim (united whites, excluded Africans) + evidence (whites held power, 80%+ denied rights) + explanation (racial exclusion built into the state) makes the case.

questions.question: Compare these two views of the Union of 1910.

source_a.text: The Union was a triumph of reconciliation, healing the wounds between Briton and Boer and bringing peace to the land.

source_b.text: The Union reconciled whites with one another by agreeing to exclude the black majority from the new nation entirely.

statements.text: The Union is praised as a triumph of reconciliation between whites
The white reconciliation was built on excluding the black majority
The black majority is named as excluded from the nation
The Union is said to have 'brought peace to the land'
Both sources judge the Union the same way

questions.memo: The settler history (A) celebrates white reconciliation; the modern account (B) shows that reconciliation was bought by excluding Africans. The 'peace' was peace among whites only.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Control of mineral wealth was central to British imperialism in South Africa.'
questions.thesis: Control of mineral wealth was central to British imperialism in South Africa.

pool.text: The world's richest gold field lay in the Boer-controlled Transvaal
Britain went to war with the Boer republics partly to control the gold of the Witwatersrand
Mining capital and the British government worked closely together to secure the mines
Britain is an island
Diamonds are very hard
Britain also had strategic interests in the Cape sea route

questions.memo: The gold lay in Boer territory (e1), Britain fought partly to control it (e2), and capital and government worked together (e3). e6 is a fair counter — strategic interests existed too — but the minerals were central.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why former British and Boer enemies cooperated to build the Union.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why British and Boer whites cooperated to build the Union.

options.text: A shared interest in ruling over the black majority drew the white groups together
They cooperated because they had always been friends
They cooperated at the request of African leaders
Just eight years after a bitter war, British and Afrikaner whites agreed at the National Convention to a white-controlled Union
Both groups lived in southern Africa
Both groups used the same money
Maintaining white control over the African majority mattered more to both groups than their differences with each other
They had simply forgotten the war
There were no real differences between them

questions.memo: Claim (shared interest in ruling the majority) + evidence (white cooperation just 8 years after the war) + explanation (white control mattered more than their mutual differences) explains the cooperation.

questions.question: Compare these two explanations of the South African War.

source_a.text: Britain fought only to protect the rights of British settlers who were being mistreated in the Boer republics.

source_b.text: At the heart of the war lay control of the world's richest gold fields on the Witwatersrand.

statements.text: The war is explained as protecting mistreated British settlers
The war is explained by the struggle for control of the gold fields
The Witwatersrand gold is named as central to the war
The war is justified as defending settlers' rights
Both sources give the same reason for the war

questions.memo: The British justification (A) cites settlers' rights; the economic history (B) points to the gold. The 'protecting settlers' story conveniently overlooked the immense mineral wealth at stake.

HIS.G12.T1.POLECON.A2.title: Racial capitalism: the colour bar, migrant labour and the 'poor white' problem
HIS.G12.T1.POLECON.A2.description: How the economy was built on racial discrimination: the 'civilised labour' policy and colour bar, job reservation at ISCOR and ESKOM, the migrant labour system, the Great Depression and the 'poor white' problem, and racially organised education.
HIS.G12.T1.POLECON.A2.strand: T1 — Politics & Economics of SA + The National Question
HIS.G12.T1.POLECON.A2.caps_topic: The Politics and Economics of South Africa in the Late 19th and 20th Centuries
HIS.G12.T1.POLECON.A2.recovery_strategy: The economy was RACIAL by design: the 'civilised labour' policy and colour bar reserved good jobs for whites; job reservation at ISCOR/ESKOM protected them; migrant labour kept African workers cheap and controlled. The state rescued poor whites (state jobs, protection) while keeping Africans poor. Inequality was legislated, not accidental.

questions.question: The 'civilised labour' policy was designed to:
options: Reserve skilled, well-paid jobs for white workers
questions.expected: Reserve skilled, well-paid jobs for white workers
questions.memo: The 'civilised labour' policy treated white workers as 'civilised' and reserved skilled, better-paid jobs for them, pushing African workers into low-paid, insecure work.

questions.question: A 'colour bar' in the workplace meant:
options: Certain jobs were reserved by law or custom for white workers only
Workers were paid in coloured tokens
Factories were painted in different colours
questions.expected: Certain jobs were reserved by law or custom for white workers only
questions.memo: The colour bar reserved skilled and supervisory jobs for whites and blocked African workers from advancing — a racial ceiling built into the economy.

questions.question: State-owned enterprises that used job reservation to protect white workers included ISCOR and _________.
questions.memo: State enterprises like ISCOR (iron and steel) and ESKOM (electricity) used job reservation to guarantee employment for white workers, especially poor whites.

questions.question: True or false: The migrant labour system supplied the mines with cheap, controllable African labour.
questions.memo: Migrant labour drew African men from rural areas and the reserves to work in the mines on short contracts, keeping wages low and workers controlled and separated from their families.

questions.question: True or false: African workers earned less mainly because they were naturally less skilled, not because of any law.
questions.memo: African workers earned less because the law and the colour bar BLOCKED them from skilled jobs and training. The inequality was created by policy, not by ability.

questions.question: The 'poor white problem' became especially severe during the _________ of the early 1930s.
questions.memo: The Great Depression of the early 1930s pushed many white Afrikaners into poverty — the 'poor white problem' — which the state addressed through job reservation and state jobs.

questions.question: Sort each measure by whether it PROTECTED white workers or CONTROLLED African workers.

items.text: Job reservation at ISCOR and ESKOM
The migrant labour system
The 'civilised labour' policy
Pass laws restricting African movement
State help for poor whites
Low wages fixed for African mine workers

questions.memo: The system worked both ways at once: it protected white workers (job reservation, civilised labour, state help) and controlled African workers (migrant labour, passes, low wages).

questions.question: Why is South Africa's economy in this period described as 'racial capitalism'?
options: Profit and economic growth were built on a system of racial discrimination
Capitalism had no connection to race
Race had no effect on wages or jobs
questions.expected: Profit and economic growth were built on a system of racial discrimination
questions.memo: 'Racial capitalism' means the pursuit of profit was organised around race — cheap, controlled African labour and protected white labour together made the system work.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to describe racial capitalism.
questions.cloze_template: The economy reserved skilled jobs for [1] workers through the colour bar and the '[2] labour' policy. African workers were kept cheap and controlled through the [3] labour system and low [4]. When the Great Depression created a '[5] white problem', the state rescued white workers with job reservation.
questions.memo: White workers protected (colour bar, civilised labour, job reservation for poor whites); African workers controlled (migrant labour, low wages). That is racial capitalism.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show this employer is defending the colour bar with racist reasoning.
questions.source_text: Skilled positions must be kept for the civilised white worker, for the native is by nature suited only to rough manual toil and would lower the standards of any trade he entered.
questions.task: Tap the phrases that use racist reasoning to justify the colour bar.

targets.phrase: kept for the civilised white worker
targets.reason: Reserves good jobs for whites by calling them 'civilised'

targets.phrase: the native is by nature suited only to rough manual toil
targets.reason: A racist claim used to block African advancement

targets.phrase: would lower the standards of any trade he entered
targets.reason: Justifies exclusion with a false claim about ability

questions.memo: Reserving jobs for the 'civilised white worker' and claiming the 'native is by nature' fit only for manual toil are racist justifications for an unfair colour bar — not statements of fact.

questions.question: Compare these two views on why African workers earned so little.

source_a.text: The native worker earns less simply because he lacks the skill and ambition of the European.

source_b.text: African workers were barred by the colour bar from skilled jobs and training, and the migrant system fixed their wages low by design.

statements.text: Low African wages are blamed on a lack of skill and ambition
Low African wages are explained by the colour bar and the migrant system
African workers are said to have been barred from training
The 'native worker' is said to lack 'skill and ambition'
Both sources explain low wages the same way

questions.memo: Management (A) blames the workers; the historian (B) shows the law and the migrant system fixed wages low. The 'lack of skill' story hid a deliberate design.

questions.question: How did the migrant labour system keep African mine wages low?
options: Workers came on short contracts from the reserves, with no bargaining power and families left behind
Workers owned the mines and chose their own pay
Workers were paid the same as white workers
Workers were given long-term, secure contracts
questions.expected: Workers came on short contracts from the reserves, with no bargaining power and families left behind
questions.memo: By drawing workers on short contracts from rural reserves and housing them in single-sex compounds away from their families, the system gave African workers little bargaining power and kept wages low.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or a MYTH about racial capitalism in this period.

items.text: The colour bar reserved skilled jobs for white workers
African workers earned less only because of natural ability
The state rescued poor whites with job reservation
Migrant labour was designed to benefit African families
Education was organised along racial lines
Inequality in the economy happened by accident

questions.memo: True: the colour bar, state help for poor whites, racial education. Myths: that low African wages came from ability, that migrant labour helped families, or that inequality was accidental.

questions.question: How did the state solve the 'poor white problem' in the 1930s?
options: By reserving jobs for whites at state enterprises like ISCOR and ESKOM
By giving poor whites no help at all
By employing them in the mines alongside Africans at equal pay
By sending them to the reserves
questions.expected: By reserving jobs for whites at state enterprises like ISCOR and ESKOM
questions.memo: The state used job reservation at enterprises like ISCOR and ESKOM, plus the colour bar, to lift poor whites out of poverty — protection it did not extend to African workers.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Inequality in South Africa's economy was created by law, not by accident.'
questions.thesis: Inequality in South Africa's economy was created by law, not by accident.

pool.text: The colour bar and 'civilised labour' policy legally reserved good jobs for whites
Job reservation at state enterprises protected white workers by design
The migrant labour system and pass laws deliberately kept African workers cheap and controlled
South Africa has a warm climate
Gold is mined deep underground
Some inequality also came from individual employers' choices

questions.memo: The colour bar (e1), job reservation (e2), and migrant labour/passes (e3) were all legal structures creating inequality. e6 is a fair counter — individual choices mattered too — but the system itself was built in law.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why this economy is called 'racial capitalism'.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why this economy is called 'racial capitalism'.

options.text: Profit in this economy was organised around racial discrimination
Capitalism in South Africa had nothing to do with race
Everyone shared equally in the profits
White workers were protected by the colour bar and job reservation while African workers were kept cheap by the migrant system
South Africa produced gold and steel
The economy grew over time
Because race determined who got which jobs and wages, profit and racial domination were built into the same system
Because race played no part in the economy
Because wages were the same for everyone

questions.memo: Claim (profit organised around race) + evidence (whites protected, Africans kept cheap) + explanation (race set jobs and wages, fusing profit with racial domination) explains 'racial capitalism'.

questions.question: Compare these two views of the 'poor white problem' and its solution.

source_a.text: The upliftment of the poor whites was a proud achievement of self-help and hard work by a determined people.

source_b.text: Poor whites were lifted out of poverty by state job reservation at ISCOR and ESKOM, a helping hand denied to poor Africans.

statements.text: Poor whites are said to have risen through self-help and hard work alone
Poor whites are shown rising through state job reservation
The same help was denied to poor Africans
The upliftment is called a proud achievement of a determined people
Both sources explain the rise of poor whites the same way

questions.memo: The nationalist account (A) credits self-help; the social history (B) shows the state intervened for whites only. The 'hard work' story hides the racial helping hand.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The migrant labour system was central to keeping African workers cheap and controlled.'
questions.thesis: The migrant labour system was central to keeping African workers cheap and controlled.

pool.text: Workers came on short contracts from rural reserves, with little bargaining power
They were housed in single-sex compounds, separated from their families
Pass laws controlled their movement and tied them to the labour system
The mines were located near towns
Gold is valuable
Some African workers did acquire experience and informal skills over time

questions.memo: Short contracts and weak bargaining (e1), compounds away from family (e2), and pass laws (e3) kept African labour cheap and controlled. e6 is a fair counter — workers gained experience — but the system still suppressed their wages and freedom.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why racially organised education supported racial capitalism.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why racially organised education supported racial capitalism.

options.text: Education along racial lines prepared whites and Africans for unequal roles in the economy
Education was identical for all groups
Education had no link to the economy
Schools, colleges and universities were developed separately and unequally by race
Schools had buildings
Children attended school
By giving whites better education and Africans inferior schooling, the system channelled each group toward the jobs racial capitalism reserved for them
Because education made everyone equal
Because education was unrelated to work

questions.memo: Claim (education prepared unequal roles) + evidence (separate, unequal schooling by race) + explanation (channelled each group to the jobs reserved for them) links education to racial capitalism.

questions.question: Compare these two judgements of South Africa's industrial economy in this period.

source_a.text: Industrialisation brought prosperity and modern development that benefited the whole country.

source_b.text: That prosperity rested on a colour bar and migrant labour that enriched whites while impoverishing the African majority.

statements.text: Industrialisation is praised as benefiting the whole country
The prosperity is shown to rest on the colour bar and migrant labour
The African majority is said to have been impoverished by the system
Industrialisation is said to benefit 'the whole country'
Both sources judge the economy the same way

questions.memo: The official survey (A) sees shared prosperity; the modern history (B) shows it enriched whites at Africans' expense. 'Benefited the whole country' ignores who paid the price.

HIS.G12.T1.POLECON.A3.title: Workers' struggles and the birth of three movements
HIS.G12.T1.POLECON.A3.description: How the mineral revolution gave rise to African nationalism, Afrikaner nationalism and a workers'/communist movement: the white mineworkers' revolts (1913, 1922), the 1920 African mineworkers' strike, the ICU and Clements Kadalie, the CPSA, the institutions of Afrikaner nationalism, and women's protest.
HIS.G12.T1.POLECON.A3.strand: T1 — Politics & Economics of SA + The National Question
HIS.G12.T1.POLECON.A3.caps_topic: The Politics and Economics of South Africa in the Late 19th and 20th Centuries
HIS.G12.T1.POLECON.A3.recovery_strategy: The same mining economy bred THREE responses: African nationalism, Afrikaner nationalism, and a workers'/communist movement. Keep the revolts straight: white miners revolted in 1913 and 1922; African miners struck in 1920; the ICU (Kadalie) organised African workers. Afrikaner nationalism worked through the Broederbond, FAK and DRC. Women resisted too (1913 anti-pass, Charlotte Maxeke).

questions.question: The Industrial and Commercial Workers' Union (ICU) was led by:
questions.memo: Clements Kadalie led the ICU, formed in 1921 — one of the first mass movements organising African (and other) workers.

questions.question: The Communist Party of South Africa was influenced by which 1917 event?
options: The end of the South African War
questions.memo: The 1917 Russian Revolution and the founding of the USSR inspired the formation of the Communist Party of South Africa in 1921.

questions.question: A key organisation promoting Afrikaner nationalism in secret was the Afrikaner _________.
questions.memo: The Afrikaner Broederbond (a secret society), along with the FAK and the Dutch Reformed Church, drove the cultural and political project of Afrikaner nationalism.

questions.question: True or false: White mineworkers staged major revolts in 1913 and 1922.
questions.memo: White mineworkers revolted in 1913 and again in the 1922 Rand Revolt, partly to defend the colour bar and their privileged position against mine owners cutting costs.

questions.question: African mineworkers staged a major strike in _________.
questions.memo: African mineworkers struck in 1920, demanding better wages and conditions — an early mass action by African workers against the racial labour system.

questions.question: True or false: The mineral revolution gave rise to African nationalism, Afrikaner nationalism and a workers' movement at the same time.
questions.memo: The same industrial economy produced all three responses — African nationalism, Afrikaner nationalism and a communist/workers' movement — each reacting to the new order in its own way.

questions.question: Sort each item by the movement it belongs to.

items.text: The ICU under Clements Kadalie
The Afrikaner Broederbond
The CPSA, inspired by the 1917 Russian Revolution
The FAK and the Dutch Reformed Church
The 1920 African mineworkers' strike
A movement organising workers across racial lines around class

questions.memo: African (ICU, 1920 strike); Afrikaner (Broederbond, FAK, DRC); communist (CPSA, class-based worker organising). Three distinct responses to the same economy.

questions.question: What did the white mineworkers' revolts of 1913 and 1922 mainly defend?
options: Their privileged, protected position and the colour bar
questions.expected: Their privileged, protected position and the colour bar
questions.memo: White miners revolted to protect their well-paid, colour-bar-protected jobs when mine owners tried to cut costs by employing cheaper African labour in skilled roles.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to compare the workers' movements.
questions.cloze_template: [1] mineworkers revolted in 1913 and 1922 to defend the colour bar, while [2] mineworkers struck in 1920 for better wages. The [3], led by Clements Kadalie, organised African workers. The Communist Party, founded in [4], was inspired by the Russian Revolution. Afrikaner nationalism worked through bodies like the [5].
questions.memo: White revolts (1913, 1922) defended the colour bar; African strike (1920); ICU (Kadalie) for African workers; CPSA (1921); Afrikaner nationalism via the Broederbond.

questions.question: Place these events in chronological order — earliest first.

items.text: Women's anti-pass protests (1913)
The 1917 Russian Revolution inspires South African socialists
The African mineworkers' strike (1920)
The formation of the ICU under Clements Kadalie (1921)

questions.memo: 1913 anti-pass protests → 1917 Russian Revolution → 1920 African strike → 1921 ICU. The 1910s–20s were a period of rising worker and political organisation.

questions.question: Who spearheaded the 1913 women's protests against passes and is linked to early African women's organisation?
questions.memo: Charlotte Maxeke was a leading figure in early African women's organisation and protest, including resistance to passes for women.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on the workers' movements.

source_a.text: The white miners rose up to protect their hard-won rights against greedy mine owners.

source_b.text: African workers organising in bodies like the ICU faced both the mine owners and a colour bar that white workers fought to keep.

statements.text: White miners are praised for protecting their rights
African workers faced both the owners and the colour bar
White workers are said to have fought to keep the colour bar
The white miners' cause is presented sympathetically against 'greedy' owners
Both sources describe the same struggle in the same way

questions.memo: The white labour paper (A) frames the white miners as heroes; the historian (B) notes their fight preserved a colour bar that hurt African workers. Same events, very different sympathies.

questions.question: Why did the CPSA's focus on class sometimes sit uneasily with movements focused on race or nation?
options: It emphasised workers' shared class interests across racial lines, while others organised around race or nation
It refused to organise any workers
It was identical to Afrikaner nationalism
questions.expected: It emphasised workers' shared class interests across racial lines, while others organised around race or nation
questions.memo: The communist movement stressed class unity across race, while African and Afrikaner nationalisms organised around national and racial identity — a tension that ran through South African politics.

questions.question: Which institutions did Afrikaner nationalism use to build its strength?
options: The Broederbond, the FAK and the Dutch Reformed Church
The mines and the trade unions of African workers
questions.expected: The Broederbond, the FAK and the Dutch Reformed Church
questions.memo: Afrikaner nationalism advanced through the secret Broederbond, the cultural FAK, and the Dutch Reformed Church — building a network that would later carry the National Party to power.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The mineral revolution gave birth to three rival movements at once.'
questions.thesis: The mineral revolution gave birth to three rival movements at once: African nationalism, Afrikaner nationalism and a workers' movement.

pool.text: African workers and the excluded majority organised through bodies like the ICU and early nationalism
Aggrieved Afrikaners built a nationalist project through the Broederbond, FAK and DRC
Industrial workers organised around class through the CPSA and trade unions
South Africa produced a lot of gold
Mines were located on the Witwatersrand
The three movements sometimes overlapped and influenced one another

questions.memo: African organisation (e1), Afrikaner nationalism (e2), and the class-based workers' movement (e3) all grew from the same industrial economy. e6 is a fair counter — they overlapped — but they were three distinct, often rival, responses.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why white miners revolted to defend the colour bar.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why white miners revolted to defend the colour bar.

options.text: White miners revolted to protect their privileged, protected jobs
White miners revolted to win rights for African workers
White miners revolted for no reason
When mine owners tried to cut costs by using cheaper African labour in skilled jobs, white miners rose up in 1913 and 1922
Mines are deep underground
Gold was valuable
The colour bar guaranteed white workers well-paid jobs, so they fought to keep African workers out of skilled positions
They wanted to abolish all racial privilege
They had no interest in their wages

questions.memo: Claim (protect privileged jobs) + evidence (revolted when owners used cheaper African labour) + explanation (colour bar guaranteed their jobs) explains the white miners' revolts.

questions.question: Compare these two views of the ICU.

source_a.text: The ICU was a dangerous agitating body that stirred up the contented native worker.

source_b.text: The ICU was the first mass movement to give African workers a collective voice against low wages and the colour bar.

statements.text: The ICU is condemned as a dangerous agitating body
The ICU is described as giving African workers a collective voice
African workers are said to have been 'contented' before the ICU
The ICU is linked to resisting low wages and the colour bar
Both sources judge the ICU the same way

questions.memo: The government (A) calls the ICU a dangerous agitator and imagines 'contented' workers; the historian (B) recognises it as the first mass African workers' movement. The 'contented worker' was a comfortable official fiction.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'African workers actively resisted the racial labour system, despite great obstacles.'
questions.thesis: African workers actively resisted the racial labour system, despite great obstacles.

pool.text: African mineworkers staged a major strike in 1920
The ICU under Kadalie organised African workers into a mass movement
Women protested against passes, as in 1913, despite harsh penalties
South Africa had many mines
Johannesburg grew quickly
The colour bar and pass laws made organising extremely difficult

questions.memo: The 1920 strike (e1), the ICU (e2), and women's anti-pass protest (e3) show active resistance. e6 is a fair counter — the obstacles were severe — but that makes the resistance more remarkable, not less real.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why the same economy produced both African and Afrikaner nationalism.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why the same economy produced both African and Afrikaner nationalism.

options.text: Different groups responded to the same industrial order by building rival nationalisms
Only one group ever responded to the economy
The economy had no effect on politics
Excluded Africans organised for inclusion, while aggrieved Afrikaners organised to advance their own position within the white state
Both groups lived in South Africa
Both groups spoke languages
Because the mineral economy reshaped everyone's lives, each group built a nationalism to defend or advance its interests within it
Because the groups had identical interests
Because nationalism had nothing to do with the economy

questions.memo: Claim (rival nationalisms from one order) + evidence (Africans organised for inclusion, Afrikaners to advance within the white state) + explanation (each built a nationalism to defend its interests) answers the question.

questions.question: Compare these two views on the role of women in early resistance.

source_a.text: Politics in this era was the work of men; women played no real part in the struggles of the time.

source_b.text: Women like Charlotte Maxeke led anti-pass protests as early as 1913 and built lasting organisations.

statements.text: Women are said to have played no real part in the struggles
Women are shown leading anti-pass protests and building organisations
Charlotte Maxeke is named as a leader of protest
Politics is described as 'the work of men'
Both sources describe women's role the same way

questions.memo: The older textbook (A) erases women; the modern history (B) records leaders like Charlotte Maxeke and the 1913 anti-pass protests. Leaving women out gives a false picture of the resistance.

HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A1.title: What the 'national question' was — and the exclusion built into the Union
HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A1.description: The national question — who counts as a South African and who holds power. The Treaty of Vereeniging (1902), the whites-only National Convention (1907–08), and the Union of 1910 excluding over 80% of people. Segregation versus apartheid, and the competing liberal, Marxist, Afrikaner-nationalist, Africanist and African-nationalist interpretations.
HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A1.strand: T1 — Politics & Economics of SA + The National Question
HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A1.caps_topic: The National Question in South Africa: the formation of the ANC, the National Party, the Communist Party of South Africa and other organisations
HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A1.recovery_strategy: The 'national question' asks: in a country where oppressor and oppressed share the same space, who counts as a citizen and who holds power? At Union (1910), built on Vereeniging (1902) and a whites-only Convention, over 80% of people were locked out of citizenship. Different camps (liberal, Marxist, Africanist, African-nationalist) answered the question very differently.

questions.question: The 'national question' in South Africa was essentially about:
options: Who counts as a South African and who holds political power
questions.expected: Who counts as a South African and who holds political power
questions.memo: The national question asks who belongs to the nation and who holds power in a state shared by oppressor and oppressed — a debate that ran from 1910 to 1994.

questions.question: The Treaty of Vereeniging in 1902:
options: Ended the South African War and began British–Afrikaner cooperation
questions.expected: Ended the South African War and began British–Afrikaner cooperation
questions.memo: The Treaty of Vereeniging (1902) ended the war and laid the basis for British and Afrikaner whites to cooperate in building a white state.

questions.question: The National Convention that planned the Union (1907–08) was open to _________ only.
questions.memo: The National Convention was a whites-only affair. The state it designed excluded the African majority from the start.

questions.question: True or false: The Union of 1910 excluded over 80% of South Africa's population from citizenship rights.
questions.memo: The black majority — over 80% of the population — was excluded from citizenship and political rights in the new Union, which is the root of the national question.

questions.question: A striking feature of the South African system between 1910 and 1994 was that:
options: The oppressor and the oppressed lived in the same country
The oppressed lived on a different continent
There was no oppression at all
questions.expected: The oppressor and the oppressed lived in the same country
questions.memo: Unlike a distant colony, here oppressor and oppressed shared the same geographical space — which made the question of who belonged to the nation especially fierce.

questions.question: True or false: All historians and activists agreed on a single answer to the national question.
questions.memo: There were competing interpretations — liberal, Marxist, Afrikaner-nationalist, Africanist and African-nationalist — each answering the national question differently.

questions.question: Sort each statement about the Union of 1910 as TRUE or FALSE.

items.text: It united British and Afrikaner whites
It gave the African majority the vote
It grew out of the Treaty of Vereeniging (1902)
It was planned at a convention open to everyone
It excluded over 80% of the population from citizenship
It resolved the national question fairly for all

questions.memo: True: united whites, grew from Vereeniging, excluded 80%+. False: gave Africans the vote, open convention, fair for all.

questions.question: Why did liberal thinkers consider the national question 'resolved' from 1910, despite the exclusion of most people?
options: They saw a single white-led economy and state as the basis of nationhood, including others only slowly on 'white standards'
They believed everyone already had equal rights
They thought South Africa had no white people
They opposed any nation-state at all
questions.expected: They saw a single white-led economy and state as the basis of nationhood, including others only slowly on 'white standards'
questions.memo: Liberals treated the white-dominated state as the nation, planning to admit black people only gradually and on 'white standards' — a qualified, not universal, franchise.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to explain the national question.
questions.cloze_template: The national question asked who counts as a [1] and who holds [2]. The Union of [3], built on the whites-only National Convention, excluded over [4]% of the population. Different schools of thought — liberal, Marxist, Africanist and African-nationalist — [5] on how to answer it.
questions.memo: Who is a South African and who holds power; the 1910 Union excluded 80%+; the schools of thought disagreed sharply.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show this liberal writer still treats white people as superior even while claiming to help black people.
questions.source_text: We must in time extend the franchise to the native, but only as he rises by instalments to meet the standards of the more civilised European, who must guide him toward the responsibilities of citizenship.
questions.task: Tap the phrases that reveal an assumption of white superiority.

targets.phrase: only as he rises by instalments
targets.reason: Inclusion is conditional and gradual, not equal

targets.phrase: the standards of the more civilised European
targets.reason: Treats Europeans as the measure of civilisation

targets.phrase: who must guide him toward the responsibilities of citizenship
targets.reason: Casts white people as superior guides over black people

questions.memo: Even this 'helpful' liberal view assumes black people must rise to 'white standards' under white 'guidance' — superiority dressed up as kindness.

questions.question: Compare these two views on the Union of 1910.

source_a.text: With Union, the national question was settled: South Africa became one nation with one government.

source_b.text: Union settled nothing for the black majority, who were locked out of the nation it created.

statements.text: The national question is said to be settled by Union
Union is said to have settled nothing for the black majority
The black majority is described as locked out of the nation
South Africa is described as 'one nation with one government'
Both sources agree on what Union achieved

questions.memo: The liberal view (A) calls the question settled; the modern view (B) shows it was unresolved for the excluded majority. 'One nation' meant one white nation.

questions.question: What is the difference, in this debate, between a 'qualified' and a 'universal' franchise?
options: A qualified franchise only lets people vote if they meet conditions; a universal one is for all adults
They mean exactly the same thing
A universal franchise excludes most people
A qualified franchise gives everyone the vote at once
questions.expected: A qualified franchise only lets people vote if they meet conditions; a universal one is for all adults
questions.memo: Liberals campaigned for a 'qualified' franchise (vote only if you meet education or property tests) — not the universal adult franchise that true democracy requires.

questions.question: Sort each interpretation of the national question to its core emphasis.

items.text: A gradual, qualified franchise within a white-led state
Class and economic exploitation at the centre of the question
Africa for Africans and full African self-determination
Capitalism and racial oppression seen as linked
Bringing black people into nationhood 'by instalments'
A democratic state belonging to its African majority

questions.memo: Liberal = gradual qualified inclusion in a white-led state. Marxist = class and economic exploitation. Africanist/African-nationalist = self-determination and a democratic state for the majority.

questions.question: Why does the national question remain relevant to South Africa long after 1994?
options: Political freedom was won in 1994, but debates about belonging and economic inequality continue
It only ever mattered to historians
It disappeared after the South African War
questions.expected: Political freedom was won in 1994, but debates about belonging and economic inequality continue
questions.memo: 1994 brought political inclusion, but questions of nationhood and the deep economic inequalities inherited from the past keep the national question alive.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The Union of 1910 created the national question rather than resolving it.'
questions.thesis: The Union of 1910 created the national question rather than resolving it.

pool.text: The Union excluded over 80% of the population from citizenship
It was designed by a whites-only convention with no black input
Its exclusions sparked the formation of African and other political organisations
The Union was formed in 1910
South Africa has nine provinces today
White liberals at the time claimed the question was settled

questions.memo: Mass exclusion (e1), whites-only design (e2), and the organisations it provoked (e3) show Union created the question. e6 is a fair counter — liberals claimed it was settled — but that claim ignored the excluded majority.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining what the 'national question' means.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining what the 'national question' means.

options.text: The national question asks who belongs to the nation and who holds power
The national question is about which crops to grow
The national question is only about language
In a country where oppressor and oppressed shared the same space, the 1910 Union granted citizenship to whites and denied it to the majority
South Africa is a large country
The Union had a flag
Because power and belonging were defined by race, who counted as a South African became the central political struggle
Because everyone already agreed who belonged
Because the question had no real consequences

questions.memo: Claim (who belongs and who holds power) + evidence (1910 gave citizenship to whites, denied it to the majority) + explanation (race defined belonging, making it the central struggle) defines the national question.

questions.question: Compare these two interpretations of the national question.

source_a.text: The real issue was always class: workers of all colours exploited by mining capital.

source_b.text: The real issue was race and nationhood: who would belong to and govern the South African nation.

statements.text: The question is framed mainly around class and exploitation
The question is framed mainly around race and nationhood
Workers of all colours are emphasised as the key actors
Belonging to and governing the nation is emphasised
Both writers frame the question identically

questions.memo: The Marxist (A) centres class; the African-nationalist (B) centres race and nationhood. Both capture part of the truth — the national question involved both class and race.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'There was no single answer to the national question — it depended on where you stood.'
questions.thesis: There was no single answer to the national question; it depended on where you stood.

pool.text: Liberals wanted gradual, qualified inclusion within a white-led state
Marxists put class exploitation at the centre of the question
Africanists demanded full self-determination and a state for the majority
South Africa has a long coastline
The Union was formed in winter
All these schools agreed apartheid was unjust

questions.memo: Liberal (e1), Marxist (e2) and Africanist (e3) answers differed fundamentally. e6 is a fair counter — they shared opposition to injustice — but they disagreed deeply on the answer itself.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why the whites-only National Convention shaped the national question.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why the whites-only National Convention shaped the national question.

options.text: Because only whites designed the Union, the new state was built to exclude the majority
The Convention included all South Africans equally
The Convention had no influence on the Union
The 1907–08 Convention that planned the Union was open to whites only, and the Union it created denied the majority citizenship
The Convention met in a building
South Africa joined the British Empire
A state designed only by those it would privilege was bound to entrench exclusion, setting up the national question for decades
Because the Convention was fair to all
Because conventions never matter

questions.memo: Claim (whites-only design built exclusion in) + evidence (whites-only Convention, majority denied citizenship) + explanation (a state designed by the privileged entrenched exclusion) makes the case.

questions.question: Compare these two views on whether 1994 ended the national question.

source_a.text: With the democratic election of 1994, the national question was finally and fully resolved.

source_b.text: 1994 delivered political freedom, but deep economic inequalities left key parts of the national question unresolved.

statements.text: 1994 is said to have fully resolved the national question
1994 is said to have delivered political freedom but left economic inequality
Deep economic inequalities are named as unresolved
The national question is said to be 'finally and fully resolved'
Both sources agree the question was fully resolved

questions.memo: The celebratory view (A) sees full resolution in 1994; the analysis (B) shows political freedom came but economic inequality persisted. The national question had a political answer in 1994 and an unfinished economic one.

HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A2.title: The organisations form: ANC, NP, CPSA and others
HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A2.description: The political organisations born from exclusion: the SANNC (1912, later the ANC), the National Party (1914), the Indian congresses and the APO (1902, Abdurahman), and the CPSA (1921) with its 'Native Republic Thesis' (1928). Who each represented and why each formed.
HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A2.strand: T1 — Politics & Economics of SA + The National Question
HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A2.caps_topic: The National Question in South Africa: the formation of the ANC, the National Party, the Communist Party of South Africa and other organisations
HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A2.recovery_strategy: Match each organisation to its people and purpose: SANNC/ANC (1912) — Africans excluded from the Union; NP (1914) — aggrieved Afrikaners; NIC/APO — Indian and Coloured people; CPSA (1921) — workers, later embracing the 'Native Republic Thesis' (1928). They formed in response to the SAME exclusion but wanted very different futures.

questions.question: The organisation founded in 1912 that later became the ANC was the:
questions.memo: The SANNC was founded in January 1912 to unite Africans against their exclusion from the Union; it was later renamed the African National Congress (ANC).

questions.question: The National Party, formed in 1914, mainly represented:
questions.memo: The National Party (1914) expressed Afrikaner grievance and nationalism within the white state.

questions.question: The Communist Party of South Africa was founded in _________.
questions.memo: The CPSA was founded in 1921, growing out of class contradictions in the South African economy and inspired by the 1917 Russian Revolution.

questions.question: True or false: The SANNC was formed because Africans had been excluded from the Union of 1910.
questions.memo: After the 1908–10 campaign for inclusion failed, Africans came together to form the SANNC in 1912 — a direct response to exclusion from the Union.

questions.question: The African People's Organisation (APO), formed in 1902, was led from 1904 by:
questions.memo: Dr Abdullah Abdurahman led the APO, the leading political organisation among Coloured people, from 1904.

questions.question: In 1928 the CPSA adopted the _________ Thesis, shifting its focus toward the national question.
questions.memo: The 'Native Republic Thesis' (1928) committed the CPSA to a 'native republic' as a stage toward socialism, engaging the national question for the first time.

questions.question: Match each organisation to the group it mainly represented.

items.text: The SANNC (later ANC)
The National Party
The Natal Indian Congress
The African People's Organisation (APO)
The organisation led by John Dube and other early African leaders
The party expressing Afrikaner grievance

questions.memo: SANNC/ANC — Africans; NP — Afrikaners; NIC and APO — Indian and Coloured South Africans. Each spoke for a different excluded or aggrieved group.

questions.question: What did these very different organisations have in common in their origins?
options: Each formed in response to the exclusions and pressures created by the white state and economy
They were all founded by the same person
They all wanted exactly the same future
They were all banned from the start
questions.expected: Each formed in response to the exclusions and pressures created by the white state and economy
questions.memo: Though they wanted very different things, all these organisations arose in response to the same context — the exclusions and pressures of the Union and the mining economy.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to summarise the founding of the organisations.
questions.cloze_template: Excluded from the Union, Africans formed the [1] in 1912. Aggrieved Afrikaners formed the [2] in 1914. Indian and Coloured people organised through the Natal Indian Congress and the [3]. The [4] Party formed in 1921 and in 1928 adopted the [5] Republic Thesis.
questions.memo: SANNC (1912, Africans), NP (1914, Afrikaners), APO/NIC (Coloured/Indian), CPSA (1921) with the Native Republic Thesis (1928).

questions.question: Place these foundings in chronological order — earliest first.

items.text: The African People's Organisation (APO) is founded (1902)
The SANNC (later ANC) is founded (1912)
The National Party is founded (1914)
The Communist Party of South Africa is founded (1921)

questions.memo: APO (1902) → SANNC (1912) → NP (1914) → CPSA (1921). A wave of organisation as different groups responded to the new white state.

questions.question: Why did the CPSA largely avoid the national question in its early years?
options: It first focused on class and white workers before the 1928 Native Republic Thesis shifted its focus
It was banned from discussing anything
It only cared about foreign affairs
questions.expected: It first focused on class and white workers before the 1928 Native Republic Thesis shifted its focus
questions.memo: In its early years the CPSA concentrated on class and had significant white membership; only with the 1928 Native Republic Thesis did it centre the national question and Black majority rule.

questions.question: The SANNC was renamed the African National Congress (ANC). What does the change of name reflect?
options: A continuing organisation representing African political aspirations
A completely new and unrelated body
A merger with the National Party
questions.expected: A continuing organisation representing African political aspirations
questions.memo: The SANNC and the ANC are the same continuing organisation under different names — the body founded in 1912 to advance African political rights.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or a MYTH about the founding of these organisations.

items.text: The SANNC was founded in 1912
The National Party represented African workers
The APO organised mainly among Coloured people
All these organisations wanted the same future
The CPSA adopted the Native Republic Thesis in 1928
The ANC and the National Party were the same party

questions.memo: True: SANNC 1912, APO for Coloured people, CPSA's 1928 thesis. Myths: NP for African workers, identical goals, ANC = NP.

questions.question: How did the goals of the SANNC and the National Party fundamentally differ?
options: The SANNC sought African inclusion and rights; the NP sought to advance Afrikaner power within a white state
Both wanted to abolish the white state

HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A3.title: From segregation to apartheid and the Bantustans
HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A3.description: The hardening of segregation into apartheid after 1948, and the Bantustan (homeland) strategy used to strip Africans of South African citizenship and deny the majority any claim to the country as a whole.
HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A3.strand: T1 — Politics & Economics of SA + The National Question
HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A3.caps_topic: The National Question in South Africa: the formation of the ANC, the National Party, the Communist Party of South Africa and other organisations
HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A3.recovery_strategy: Apartheid (from 1948) was segregation made harsher and more systematic. The Bantustans were the key trick: by assigning Africans to ethnic 'homelands', the state could strip them of South African citizenship and claim the rest of the country for whites. The homelands were a tool of dispossession, not a gift of self-rule.

questions.question: In which year did the National Party come to power and begin to impose apartheid?
questions.memo: The National Party won the 1948 election and began building apartheid — a harsher, more systematic version of the segregation that came before.

questions.question: Apartheid is best described as:
options: A more systematic and rigid intensification of earlier segregation
A system of equal rights for all
A brief experiment that changed nothing
The same as the Union of 1910
questions.expected: A more systematic and rigid intensification of earlier segregation
questions.memo: Apartheid did not appear from nowhere: it built on and intensified the segregation already in place, making racial separation far more rigid and total.

questions.question: The ethnic 'homelands' created to house Africans were also called _________.
questions.memo: The 'homelands' or Bantustans were territories assigned to African ethnic groups, central to apartheid's plan to deny Africans South African citizenship.

questions.question: True or false: The Bantustans were created mainly to give African peoples genuine independent countries for their own benefit.
questions.memo: The Bantustans were a tool of dispossession: by assigning Africans to ethnic 'homelands', the state stripped them of South African citizenship while keeping the wealth and land for whites.

questions.question: The main purpose of the Bantustan strategy was to:
options: Deny Africans South African citizenship by making them 'citizens' of homelands
Give Africans the best land in the country
Unite all South Africans into one nation
questions.expected: Deny Africans South African citizenship by making them 'citizens' of homelands
questions.memo: By declaring Africans citizens of separate 'homelands', the apartheid state aimed to remove their claim to South Africa itself — a way of answering the national question by excluding the majority entirely.

questions.question: True or false: There is debate among historians over whether apartheid was truly different from earlier segregation, or just more extreme.
questions.memo: Historians debate whether apartheid was a sharp break from segregation or simply its intensification — a genuine question raised in the CAPS curriculum.

questions.question: Sort each feature as belonging to SEGREGATION (before 1948), APARTHEID (after 1948), or BOTH.

items.text: Racial separation in law and land
The systematic Bantustan/homeland policy
Rigid, total classification of the whole population by race
Exclusion of Africans from political power
Earlier, less systematic forms of racial division
White control of land and the economy

questions.memo: Both shared racial separation and African exclusion. Apartheid added the systematic Bantustan policy and total racial classification — segregation was the looser earlier form.

questions.question: How did the Bantustans connect to the national question?
options: They were apartheid's attempt to answer it by removing Africans from the nation altogether
They gave Africans equal say in the nation
They had nothing to do with citizenship
They made South Africa a democracy
questions.expected: They were apartheid's attempt to answer it by removing Africans from the nation altogether
questions.memo: The national question asked who belongs to the nation. Apartheid's answer, through the Bantustans, was to declare Africans belonged to separate 'homelands', not to South Africa.

questions.memo: From 1948, segregation → apartheid; the Bantustan strategy stripped Africans of citizenship while keeping the land and wealth for whites.

questions.memo: The impoverished homelands forced people to seek work in white South Africa as migrant labourers — linking the Bantustan policy directly to the cheap-labour economy.

questions.thesis: The Bantustans were a tool of dispossession, not genuine self-rule.

HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A4.title: Alternative visions: Sobukwe, the PAC and Black Consciousness
HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A4.description: Different imaginations of a free South Africa beyond the ANC's: Robert Sobukwe and the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), and Steve Biko and the Black Consciousness Movement (BCM) and AZAPO in the 1970s — psychological liberation, African self-reliance and competing definitions of freedom.
HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A4.strand: T1 — Politics & Economics of SA + The National Question
HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A4.caps_topic: The National Question in South Africa: the formation of the ANC, the National Party, the Communist Party of South Africa and other organisations
HIS.G12.T1.NATQ.A4.recovery_strategy: The liberation struggle had MORE than one vision. Sobukwe's PAC offered an Africanist alternative to the ANC. Biko's Black Consciousness Movement (1970s) and AZAPO stressed psychological liberation and Black self-reliance. Keep them apart: Sobukwe = PAC (Pan-Africanist); Biko = Black Consciousness/AZAPO. Each answered the national question differently.

questions.question: Robert Sobukwe was the founding leader of which organisation?
questions.memo: Robert Sobukwe led the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), which broke from the ANC to advance an Africanist vision.

questions.question: Steve Biko is associated with which movement?
questions.memo: Steve Biko was the leading figure of the Black Consciousness Movement (BCM), which rose in the 1970s.

questions.question: The Black Consciousness-aligned organisation formed in the 1970s was _________.
questions.memo: The Azanian People's Organisation (AZAPO) was a key Black Consciousness organisation. (The PAC, by contrast, was Sobukwe's Africanist body.)

questions.question: True or false: The PAC and the Black Consciousness Movement offered alternative visions to the ANC's.
questions.memo: The liberation struggle was not a single movement. The PAC and the BCM each offered their own vision of liberation, distinct from the ANC's.

questions.memo: Biko argued that liberation had to begin in the mind: black people had to reject the sense of inferiority apartheid imposed and build pride and self-reliance.

questions.question: The PAC's outlook is best described as _________.
questions.memo: The PAC was Africanist — it stressed African leadership and self-determination, a future South Africa governed by and for its African majority.

questions.question: Match each idea to the right movement.

Emphasised African self-determination and leadership
Stressed black pride and self-reliance

questions.memo: PAC (Sobukwe): Africanist, African self-determination. BCM (Biko): psychological liberation, black pride and self-reliance, inspiring AZAPO.

questions.question: Why did the existence of the PAC and BCM matter for the national question?
options: They showed there was more than one vision of who the free nation would belong to and how to get there
They proved everyone agreed with the ANC
They had no ideas of their own
questions.expected: They showed there was more than one vision of who the free nation would belong to and how to get there
questions.memo: The PAC and BCM enriched and complicated the national question, offering different answers about the nature of liberation and the future South African nation.

questions.memo: Sobukwe → PAC (Africanist); Biko → Black Consciousness Movement (1970s) → inspired AZAPO.

questions.memo: The idea that the oppressor's weapon is 'the mind of the oppressed', and that one must shed 'the inferiority planted in him' to be 'truly free', is the heart of Black Consciousness.

questions.question: Compare these two visions of liberation.

source_a.text: South Africa belongs to all who live in it, black and white, in a shared non-racial nation.

questions.memo: The non-racial vision (A) imagines a shared nation; the Africanist vision (B) centres African self-determination. These were two genuine, competing answers to the national question.

questions.question: How did Black Consciousness aim to change the way black South Africans saw themselves?
options: By replacing imposed feelings of inferiority with pride, dignity and self-reliance
By teaching them to admire apartheid
By telling them to leave South Africa
questions.expected: By replacing imposed feelings of inferiority with pride, dignity and self-reliance
questions.memo: Black Consciousness sought to rebuild self-worth: rejecting the inferiority apartheid taught and replacing it with pride, dignity and reliance on black communities' own strength.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to think the whole anti-apartheid struggle was led by one organisation?
options: Several movements — ANC, PAC, BCM and others — offered different visions and methods
Because there was only ever one organisation
Because all organisations merged into one in 1948
questions.expected: Several movements — ANC, PAC, BCM and others — offered different visions and methods
questions.memo: The struggle was made up of several traditions — the ANC, the PAC, Black Consciousness and others — with different ideas about liberation. Reducing it to one organisation erases that richness.

questions.memo: Biko died in 1977 from injuries sustained in police detention — a stark example of the apartheid state's violent repression of those who challenged it.

questions.thesis: The liberation struggle contained several competing visions, not one.

questions.memo: Claim (liberation begins in the mind) + evidence (reject imposed inferiority, build pride) + explanation (mental freedom enables the claim to full freedom) captures Black Consciousness.

HIS.G12.T2.COLDWAR.A1.title: Origins and nature of the Cold War
HIS.G12.T2.COLDWAR.A1.description: Why the world split after WWII into a US-led capitalist bloc and a USSR-led socialist bloc; ideology and the nuclear arms race; why it was 'cold' (proxy wars, not direct war); NATO and the Warsaw Pact; the Berlin Wall and the Cuban Missile Crisis.
HIS.G12.T2.COLDWAR.A1.strand: T2 — Cold War & Anti-colonial Struggles + Liberation Struggles and the OAU
HIS.G12.T2.COLDWAR.A1.caps_topic: Cold War and the Rise of Anti-colonial Struggles in Southern Africa
HIS.G12.T2.COLDWAR.A1.recovery_strategy: 'Cold' = the superpowers never fought each other directly, because nuclear weapons made that suicidal. Instead it was ideology (USA capitalist vs USSR socialist), an arms race, and proxy wars fought through other countries. Anchors: NATO (West) vs Warsaw Pact (East), the Berlin Wall, the Cuban Missile Crisis.

questions.question: The Cold War was a rivalry mainly between which two superpowers?
questions.memo: After WWII, the capitalist USA and the socialist USSR emerged as rival superpowers, dividing much of the world into two blocs.

questions.question: Why is it called a 'cold' war rather than a 'hot' one?
options: The superpowers avoided direct war with each other, partly because of nuclear weapons
No fighting happened anywhere in the world
It took place in cold countries
The weapons were kept in freezers
questions.expected: The superpowers avoided direct war with each other, partly because of nuclear weapons
questions.memo: It was 'cold' because the USA and USSR never fought each other directly — nuclear weapons made that too dangerous — so the conflict ran through proxy wars, propaganda and the arms race.

questions.question: The USA led the _________ bloc, while the USSR led the socialist bloc.
questions.memo: The USA led the capitalist (Western) bloc; the USSR led the socialist (communist) bloc. Keep them straight: USA = capitalist, USSR = socialist.

questions.question: True or false: A major feature of the Cold War was a nuclear arms race between the superpowers.
questions.memo: Both sides built up huge nuclear arsenals. The fear of nuclear war is exactly why they avoided fighting each other directly.

questions.question: The Western military alliance formed during the Cold War was:
questions.memo: NATO was the Western (US-led) alliance; the Warsaw Pact was the Eastern (Soviet-led) alliance. Two blocs, two alliances.

questions.question: The 1962 crisis that brought the superpowers to the brink of nuclear war was the _________ Missile Crisis.
questions.memo: The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) was the Cold War's most dangerous moment, when the USA and USSR came close to nuclear war over missiles in Cuba.

questions.question: Sort each item by the Cold War bloc it belonged to.

items.text: The USA
The USSR
NATO
The Warsaw Pact
Capitalism
Socialism/communism

questions.memo: West: USA, NATO, capitalism. East: USSR, Warsaw Pact, socialism. Two blocs defined by ideology and alliance.

questions.question: What is a 'proxy war' in the Cold War?
options: A war fought through other, smaller countries instead of directly between the superpowers
A war fought only with words
A war that never actually involved fighting
questions.expected: A war fought through other, smaller countries instead of directly between the superpowers
questions.memo: In a proxy war the superpowers backed opposing sides in another country's conflict — fighting each other indirectly without risking direct nuclear war.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to describe the Cold War.
questions.cloze_template: After the Second World War the [1] (capitalist) and the [2] (socialist) became rival superpowers. It was a '[3]' war because they avoided fighting each other directly, fearing [4] weapons. Instead they fought [5] wars through other countries.
questions.memo: USA (capitalist) vs USSR (socialist); 'cold' because of nuclear fear; fought via proxy wars.

questions.question: Place these Cold War events in chronological order — earliest first.
