NATO is formed (1949)
The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962)
Reforms (perestroika and glasnost) begin in the USSR (1980s)

questions.memo: 1945 (war ends, rivalry begins) → 1949 (NATO) → 1962 (Cuban Missile Crisis) → 1980s (Soviet reforms before the Cold War's end).

questions.question: The Berlin Wall, built in the early Cold War, came to symbolise:
options: The division of the world into Western and Eastern blocs
The end of the Cold War
A trade route between East and West
questions.expected: The division of the world into Western and Eastern blocs
questions.memo: The Berlin Wall divided communist East Berlin from capitalist West Berlin and became the great symbol of a world split into two hostile blocs.

questions.question: Besides war, in what other ways did the superpowers compete?
options: Propaganda, espionage, the space race and even sport
They did not compete in any other way
questions.expected: Propaganda, espionage, the space race and even sport
questions.memo: The Cold War was fought on many fronts: propaganda, spying, the space race, technology and sport — a total rivalry short of direct war.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or a MYTH about the Cold War.

items.text: The USA and USSR avoided direct war with each other
The USA and USSR fought huge battles directly against one another
The Cold War involved a nuclear arms race
The Cold War had no effect outside Europe and America
It was fought partly through proxy wars
NATO and the Warsaw Pact were the same alliance

questions.memo: True: avoided direct war, arms race, proxy wars. Myths: direct superpower battles, no global effect, NATO = Warsaw Pact.

questions.question: Why did the Cold War deeply affect countries far from the USA and USSR?
options: The superpowers competed for influence everywhere, drawing other nations into their rivalry
The superpowers only cared about each other
Other countries were unaware of the Cold War
The Cold War was confined to one city
questions.expected: The superpowers competed for influence everywhere, drawing other nations into their rivalry
questions.memo: Because both sides sought allies and influence worldwide, the Cold War shaped politics, conflicts and liberation struggles across Africa, Asia and Latin America.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Nuclear weapons kept the Cold War cold.'
questions.thesis: Nuclear weapons kept the Cold War cold.

pool.text: A direct war risked mutual nuclear destruction, which both sides wanted to avoid
Instead of fighting directly, the superpowers backed opposing sides in proxy wars
Even at the Cuban Missile Crisis, both sides pulled back from the nuclear brink
Nuclear weapons are very expensive
The USA is far from the USSR
The two sides also competed in sport and space

questions.memo: Fear of mutual destruction (e1), proxy wars instead of direct war (e2), and the pullback at the Cuban Missile Crisis (e3) support the thesis. e6 is true but a side point about other forms of competition.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why the Cold War is called 'cold'.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why the Cold War is called 'cold'.

options.text: It is called 'cold' because the superpowers never fought each other directly
It is called 'cold' because no conflict happened anywhere
It is called 'cold' because of the weather
Fearing nuclear destruction, the USA and USSR fought through proxy wars, propaganda and the arms race rather than direct battle
The USA and USSR are both large countries
The Cold War lasted decades
Because a direct, 'hot' war could have meant nuclear annihilation, the rivalry stayed 'cold' — intense but indirect
Because the two sides were friends
Because nothing was ever at stake

questions.memo: Claim (no direct fighting) + evidence (proxy wars and arms race, not direct battle) + explanation (nuclear annihilation kept it indirect) explains 'cold'.

questions.question: Compare these two descriptions of the Cold War.

source_a.text: It was a noble defence of freedom by the West against the menace of communist tyranny.

source_b.text: It was a rivalry between two superpowers, each presenting its own side as the defender of freedom or justice.
source_b.provenance: Modern history of the Cold War, 2012

statements.text: The Cold War is framed as a noble Western defence of freedom
The Cold War is framed as a rivalry where each side claimed to defend freedom or justice
Communism is described as a 'menace' and 'tyranny'
Both superpowers are said to have justified themselves to their own peoples
Both sources describe the Cold War the same way

questions.memo: Western propaganda (A) tells a one-sided heroic story; the historian (B) shows both sides used the language of 'freedom'. Recognising the propaganda on each side is part of analysing the Cold War.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The Cold War was a global conflict, not just a US–Soviet quarrel.'
questions.thesis: The Cold War was a global conflict, not just a US–Soviet quarrel.

pool.text: Both superpowers sought allies and influence across Africa, Asia and Latin America
Proxy wars drew distant countries directly into the rivalry
Liberation struggles, including in southern Africa, were shaped by Cold War alignments
The USA and USSR are large countries
The Cold War involved a lot of spying
The sharpest moments of crisis still involved the two superpowers directly

questions.memo: Global influence-seeking (e1), proxy wars (e2), and shaped liberation struggles (e3) make it global. e6 is a fair counter — the superpowers were central — but the conflict reached far beyond them.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why the nuclear arms race shaped the whole character of the Cold War.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why the nuclear arms race shaped the Cold War's character.

options.text: The threat of nuclear war made direct conflict too dangerous, shaping how the rivalry was fought
Nuclear weapons had no effect on the Cold War
The arms race ended the rivalry immediately
Both sides built enough weapons to destroy each other, so a direct war risked mutual annihilation
Nuclear weapons are made of metal
The superpowers had large armies
Because neither side could risk a direct war, the rivalry was channelled into proxy wars, espionage and the arms race itself
Because nuclear weapons made war between them likely
Because the weapons were never built

questions.memo: Claim (nuclear threat shaped the rivalry) + evidence (mutual annihilation possible) + explanation (channelled into proxy wars and the arms race) makes the case.

questions.question: Compare these two views on the Cuban Missile Crisis.

source_a.text: It proved the West's firm resolve forced the cowardly Soviets to back down.

source_b.text: Both superpowers, staring at nuclear catastrophe, made secret compromises to step back from the brink.

statements.text: The crisis is told as a simple Western victory over a cowardly enemy
The crisis is shown as both sides compromising to avoid catastrophe
Secret compromises by both sides are mentioned
The Soviets are described as 'cowardly'
Both sources tell the same story

questions.memo: The Western account (A) is a triumphant, one-sided tale; the historian (B) shows both sides compromised secretly. The 'we won, they were cowards' version hides the mutual fear and dealmaking.

HIS.G12.T2.COLDWAR.A2.title: The Cold War comes to southern Africa: Angola and Cuito Cuanavale
HIS.G12.T2.COLDWAR.A2.description: How the global Cold War became a hot war in southern Africa: South Africa's 1975 invasion of Angola, the rival movements (MPLA, UNITA, FNLA) backed by opposing powers, the battle of Cuito Cuanavale (1987–88), and apartheid South Africa positioning itself as a Western Cold War ally.
HIS.G12.T2.COLDWAR.A2.strand: T2 — Cold War & Anti-colonial Struggles + Liberation Struggles and the OAU
HIS.G12.T2.COLDWAR.A2.caps_topic: Cold War and the Rise of Anti-colonial Struggles in Southern Africa
HIS.G12.T2.COLDWAR.A2.recovery_strategy: Angola was a Cold War battlefield. Match the backers: MPLA — Cuba + USSR; UNITA — apartheid South Africa; FNLA — USA + Zaire. South Africa invaded in 1975 and fought on to Cuito Cuanavale (1987–88), presenting itself as a Western Cold War ally to justify its actions.

questions.question: In 1975, which country invaded Angola, drawing southern Africa deeper into the Cold War?
questions.memo: Apartheid South Africa invaded Angola in 1975, turning the country into a major Cold War battleground.

questions.question: Which two countries backed the MPLA in Angola?
questions.memo: The MPLA was backed by Cuba and the USSR. Remember: MPLA = Cuba + Soviet support.

questions.question: Apartheid South Africa backed which Angolan movement?
questions.memo: South Africa backed UNITA (led by Jonas Savimbi). The MPLA was backed by Cuba and the USSR; the FNLA by the USA and Zaire.

questions.question: True or false: The battle of Cuito Cuanavale (1987–88) involved South African, Angolan and Cuban forces.
questions.memo: Cuito Cuanavale (1987–88) was a major battle involving the South African Defence Force against Angolan (MPLA) and Cuban forces — a turning point in the regional Cold War conflict.

questions.question: How did apartheid South Africa justify its actions in the region to Western powers?
options: By presenting itself as a Western ally fighting communism
By admitting it was simply seizing territory
By claiming to support the liberation movements
By declaring itself neutral in the Cold War
questions.expected: By presenting itself as a Western ally fighting communism
questions.memo: Apartheid South Africa marketed itself as an anti-communist bulwark for the West, using the Cold War to win sympathy and excuse its aggression and its racist system.

questions.question: The FNLA in Angola was supported by the USA and _________.
questions.memo: The FNLA (led by Holden Roberto) was backed by the USA and Zaire. Three movements, three sets of backers.

questions.question: Match each Angolan movement to its main outside backers.

items.text: Cuba and the USSR
Apartheid South Africa
The USA and Zaire
Led by Agostinho Neto
Led by Jonas Savimbi
Led by Holden Roberto

questions.memo: MPLA (Neto): Cuba + USSR. UNITA (Savimbi): South Africa. FNLA (Roberto): USA + Zaire. Each movement was a Cold War proxy.

questions.question: Why is Angola described as a 'theatre of the Cold War'?
options: Rival local movements were backed by opposing global powers, turning Angola into a Cold War battlefield
It was a place where Cold War films were made
The Cold War never reached Africa
questions.expected: Rival local movements were backed by opposing global powers, turning Angola into a Cold War battlefield
questions.memo: Because the USA, USSR, Cuba and South Africa all backed rival movements there, Angola became a stage on which the global Cold War was fought out by proxy.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to describe the Cold War in Angola.
questions.cloze_template: In [1], South Africa invaded Angola. The [2], backed by Cuba and the USSR, fought the South African-backed [3]. At the battle of [4] (1987–88), the South African Defence Force faced Angolan and [5] forces.
questions.memo: 1975 invasion; MPLA (Cuba/USSR) vs South African-backed UNITA; Cuito Cuanavale (1987–88) against Angolan and Cuban forces.

questions.question: Place these events in chronological order — earliest first.

items.text: South Africa invades Angola (1975)
The battle of Cuito Cuanavale (1987–88)
The end of the Cold War and Namibian independence (around 1990)

questions.memo: 1975 invasion → Cuito Cuanavale (1987–88) → the end of the Cold War and Namibian independence around 1990. The Angolan conflict ran across much of the late Cold War.

questions.question: How did the Cold War give apartheid South Africa cover for its actions?
options: By posing as an anti-communist ally, it hoped Western powers would overlook its racist system
The Cold War forced it to end apartheid immediately
The Cold War had no effect on South Africa
It made South Africa join the Soviet bloc
questions.expected: By posing as an anti-communist ally, it hoped Western powers would overlook its racist system
questions.memo: Apartheid South Africa used anti-communism to win Western tolerance: by fighting 'communist' liberation movements, it hoped the West would ignore or excuse its racism.

questions.question: How did the Cold War complicate the liberation struggle in southern Africa?
options: Liberation movements that took Soviet or Cuban support were branded 'communist' by their enemies
It had no effect on the liberation movements
It made the apartheid government support liberation
questions.expected: Liberation movements that took Soviet or Cuban support were branded 'communist' by their enemies
questions.memo: Because liberation movements often received Soviet and Cuban support, apartheid South Africa and its allies branded them 'communist' to discredit a struggle that was really about freedom and rights.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or a MYTH about the Cold War in southern Africa.

items.text: South Africa invaded Angola in 1975
The MPLA was backed by the USA
Cuba sent forces to support the MPLA
Cuito Cuanavale involved no foreign forces
Apartheid South Africa posed as a Western anti-communist ally
The Cold War never reached southern Africa

questions.memo: True: 1975 invasion, Cuban support for the MPLA, SA as 'anti-communist ally'. Myths: USA backing the MPLA, no foreign forces at Cuito Cuanavale, the Cold War never reaching the region.

questions.question: What was the wider significance of the battle of Cuito Cuanavale?
options: It helped shift the balance in the region and contributed to negotiations over Namibia and Angola
It had no consequences at all
It led directly to the Berlin Wall
It ended the Second World War
questions.expected: It helped shift the balance in the region and contributed to negotiations over Namibia and Angola
questions.memo: Cuito Cuanavale is widely seen as a turning point that weakened South Africa's regional position and helped open the way to negotiations, including Namibian independence.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Angola became a battlefield of the global Cold War.'
questions.thesis: Angola became a battlefield of the global Cold War.

pool.text: The MPLA was backed by Cuba and the USSR
UNITA was backed by apartheid South Africa, and the FNLA by the USA and Zaire
Foreign forces, including Cuban troops and the South African army, fought there directly
Angola is on the Atlantic coast
Angola produces oil
There were also genuine local Angolan causes behind the conflict

questions.memo: MPLA's Soviet/Cuban backing (e1), UNITA/FNLA's Western and South African backing (e2), and foreign forces fighting there (e3) make Angola a Cold War battlefield. e6 is a fair counter — local causes existed — but the global powers turned it into a Cold War theatre.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining how apartheid South Africa used the Cold War to its advantage.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining how apartheid South Africa used the Cold War to its advantage.

options.text: South Africa posed as an anti-communist ally to win Western tolerance for apartheid
South Africa joined the Soviet bloc
South Africa stayed out of the Cold War entirely
It fought 'communist-backed' movements in Angola and branded the liberation struggle communist
South Africa is in the southern hemisphere
South Africa produces gold
By framing itself as fighting communism, it hoped Western powers would overlook its racist system
Because the West openly supported apartheid for its own sake
Because the Cold War had nothing to do with South Africa

questions.memo: Claim (posed as anti-communist ally) + evidence (fought 'communist' movements, branded the struggle communist) + explanation (hoped the West would overlook apartheid) makes the case.

questions.question: Compare these two views on South Africa's role in Angola.

source_a.text: Our forces entered Angola to defend the region against the spread of Soviet communism.

source_b.text: South Africa invaded a neighbouring country to crush a liberation movement and protect apartheid, using anti-communism as cover.

statements.text: The invasion is justified as defending against communism
The invasion is described as crushing a liberation movement to protect apartheid
Anti-communism is described as a cover for other aims
The action is presented as defending the region from 'Soviet communism'
Both sources describe the invasion the same way

questions.memo: The government (A) frames the invasion as anti-communist defence; the historian (B) sees it as protecting apartheid, with anti-communism as cover. The Cold War language disguised the real aim.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The Cold War made it easier for apartheid South Africa to attack its neighbours.'
questions.thesis: The Cold War made it easier for apartheid South Africa to attack its neighbours.

pool.text: By branding targets 'communist', South Africa justified military action against them
Posing as a Western ally won it some tolerance from anti-communist powers
Cold War rivalry meant outside powers were already arming rival sides in the region
South Africa shares borders with several countries
The region has many rivers
International opposition to apartheid still grew throughout this period

questions.memo: The 'communist' label (e1), Western tolerance (e2), and an already-armed region (e3) all helped South Africa. e6 is a fair counter — opposition grew anyway — but the Cold War still gave cover for aggression.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why liberation movements often turned to the Soviet bloc and Cuba for support.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why liberation movements turned to the Soviet bloc and Cuba.

options.text: They accepted support from those willing to help, which often meant the Soviet bloc and Cuba
They turned to apartheid South Africa for support
They needed no support from anyone
Western powers often backed the apartheid state or stayed neutral, while the USSR and Cuba offered arms and training
Cuba is an island
The USSR was very large
Movements took help where they could get it, which let their enemies brand them 'communist' regardless of their actual aims
Because they wanted to spread communism above all else
Because the West gave them everything they needed

questions.memo: Claim (took support from those willing to help) + evidence (West backed apartheid or stayed neutral; USSR/Cuba offered help) + explanation (this let enemies brand them 'communist') answers the question.

questions.question: Compare these two views on the significance of Cuito Cuanavale.

source_a.text: It was a minor skirmish of no real importance to the wider course of events.

source_b.text: It shifted the regional balance and helped open the way to Namibian independence and negotiations.

statements.text: The battle is dismissed as a minor skirmish
The battle is credited with shifting the regional balance
It is linked to Namibian independence and negotiations
The battle is said to be 'of no real importance'
Both sources judge the battle's importance the same way

questions.memo: The dismissive account (A) downplays the battle; the historian (B) treats it as a turning point toward Namibian independence and talks. Its significance is itself debated by historians.

HIS.G12.T2.COLDWAR.A3.title: International solidarity and the 1973 UN vote
HIS.G12.T2.COLDWAR.A3.description: How the world turned against apartheid during the Cold War: anti-apartheid solidarity movements abroad (often opposing their own governments), the sports and cultural boycotts, the 1973 UN vote declaring apartheid a crime against humanity, and how the end of the Cold War changed the situation.
HIS.G12.T2.COLDWAR.A3.strand: T2 — Cold War & Anti-colonial Struggles + Liberation Struggles and the OAU
HIS.G12.T2.COLDWAR.A3.caps_topic: Cold War and the Rise of Anti-colonial Struggles in Southern Africa
HIS.G12.T2.COLDWAR.A3.recovery_strategy: Ordinary people abroad often opposed apartheid while their GOVERNMENTS protected it — that is what the solidarity movements (and sports/cultural boycotts) fought. In the 1973 UN vote, apartheid was declared a crime against humanity: the USSR, African and non-aligned states voted FOR; the USA and Britain voted AGAINST. The end of the Cold War later removed apartheid's 'anti-communist' excuse.

questions.question: In 1973, the United Nations passed a vote declaring apartheid:
options: A purely internal South African matter
questions.memo: The 1973 UN vote declared apartheid a crime against humanity — a major statement of international condemnation.

questions.question: In the 1973 UN vote on apartheid, the USA and Britain:
options: Were not members of the UN
questions.memo: The USA and Britain voted AGAINST declaring apartheid a crime against humanity, while the USSR, African and non-aligned countries voted in favour.

questions.question: Movements abroad that campaigned against apartheid are called the anti-apartheid _________ movements.
questions.memo: International solidarity movements in countries like the USA and Britain campaigned against apartheid, often in opposition to their own governments.

questions.question: True or false: Sports and cultural boycotts were used to isolate apartheid South Africa.
questions.memo: Sports and cultural boycotts cut apartheid South Africa off from international competition and culture, increasing pressure on the regime.

questions.question: In many Western countries, the anti-apartheid solidarity movements often clashed with:
options: Their own governments, which kept ties with South Africa
questions.expected: Their own governments, which kept ties with South Africa
questions.memo: Ordinary people in the West often opposed apartheid while their governments maintained economic and political ties with South Africa — so the movements campaigned against their own governments.

questions.question: The end of the Cold War, with the collapse of the _________, removed apartheid's 'anti-communist' excuse.
questions.memo: When the USSR dissolved and the Cold War ended, apartheid South Africa could no longer justify itself as a bulwark against communism — weakening its position.

questions.question: Sort each item as a form of PRESSURE on apartheid or a form of SUPPORT for it.

items.text: The 1973 UN vote declaring apartheid a crime against humanity
Sports and cultural boycotts
Western governments keeping trade ties with South Africa
International solidarity movements
Treating South Africa as an anti-communist ally
Economic sanctions

questions.memo: Pressure: the UN vote, boycotts, solidarity movements, sanctions. Support: Western trade ties and treating South Africa as a Cold War ally.

questions.question: Why did the 1973 UN vote matter even though it did not immediately end apartheid?
options: It put the world's moral and legal condemnation on record and strengthened the pressure campaign
It had no effect of any kind
It made apartheid legal under international law
questions.expected: It put the world's moral and legal condemnation on record and strengthened the pressure campaign
questions.memo: Declaring apartheid a crime against humanity gave the anti-apartheid cause powerful moral and legal weight, fuelling boycotts, sanctions and solidarity worldwide.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to describe international pressure on apartheid.
questions.cloze_template: In [1] the UN declared apartheid a crime against [2], with the USSR and African states voting in favour and the [3] and Britain against. Around the world, anti-apartheid [4] movements and sports and cultural [5] increased the pressure.
questions.memo: 1973 UN vote (crime against humanity; USA + Britain against), plus solidarity movements and boycotts.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show this campaigner is opposing their OWN government's support for apartheid.

targets.reason: Names the economic and military support given by their government

questions.memo: Targeting 'our own ministers in London' who 'shake their hands', 'buy their gold' and 'arm their police' shows the solidarity movement was fighting its own government's complicity, not just Pretoria.

questions.question: Compare these two views on the international response to apartheid.

source_a.text: The free world stood united in firm opposition to apartheid from the very beginning.

source_b.text: While ordinary people and many states condemned apartheid, powers like the USA and Britain long kept ties with Pretoria.

statements.text: The 'free world' is said to have opposed apartheid united from the start

A distinction is drawn between ordinary people and their governments
Opposition is described as firm and united 'from the very beginning'
Both sources describe the response the same way

questions.memo: The simplified account (A) imagines united opposition; the historian (B) shows ordinary people opposed apartheid while their governments kept ties. The 'united free world' story is too flattering.

questions.question: How did the sports boycott put pressure on white South Africa specifically?
options: Sport mattered greatly to many white South Africans, so exclusion was keenly felt
White South Africans did not care about sport
It affected only African South Africans
It had no symbolic or real effect
questions.expected: Sport mattered greatly to many white South Africans, so exclusion was keenly felt
questions.memo: Sport was hugely important to white South African identity, so being barred from international competition was a visible, painful sign of the country's isolation.

questions.question: Why was the 1973 UN vote split along Cold War and colonial lines?
options: Newly independent and socialist states condemned apartheid, while some Western powers protected a Cold War ally
Everyone voted exactly the same way
The vote was about trade tariffs
African states voted to support apartheid
questions.expected: Newly independent and socialist states condemned apartheid, while some Western powers protected a Cold War ally
questions.memo: The vote reflected the world's divisions: African, non-aligned and socialist states condemned apartheid; some Western powers, valuing South Africa as a Cold War ally, voted against.

questions.question: How did the end of the Cold War weaken apartheid South Africa's position?
options: It could no longer justify itself as a Western shield against communism
It made the liberation movements give up
It had no effect at all
questions.expected: It could no longer justify itself as a Western shield against communism
questions.memo: With the USSR gone and the communist 'threat' over, apartheid South Africa lost its main argument for Western tolerance — adding pressure toward negotiations.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'International pressure helped isolate and weaken apartheid South Africa.'
questions.thesis: International pressure helped isolate and weaken apartheid South Africa.

pool.text: The 1973 UN vote condemned apartheid as a crime against humanity
Sports and cultural boycotts cut South Africa off from international life
Solidarity movements and sanctions pressured governments and the economy
South Africa has a long coastline
The UN headquarters is in New York
Some Western powers continued trading with South Africa for years

questions.memo: The UN condemnation (e1), boycotts (e2), and solidarity/sanctions (e3) all isolated apartheid. e6 is a fair counter — some powers kept trading — but the overall pressure still grew and bit.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining the gap between Western governments and their own citizens on apartheid.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining the gap between Western governments and their citizens on apartheid.

options.text: Many Western citizens opposed apartheid while their governments kept ties with it
Western governments and citizens fully agreed on apartheid
No one in the West cared about apartheid
Solidarity movements campaigned against their own governments, which kept trading with and arming South Africa
The West has many countries
Apartheid was in South Africa
Cold War interests and economic ties led some governments to protect apartheid even as their citizens condemned it
Because citizens and governments always agree
Because no one was paying attention

questions.memo: Claim (citizens opposed, governments kept ties) + evidence (movements campaigned against their own governments) + explanation (Cold War and economic interests) explains the gap.

questions.question: Compare these two views on the sports boycott.

source_a.text: Mixing politics with sport was unfair and achieved nothing but spoiling the game.

source_b.text: The boycott struck at something white South Africans deeply valued and made their isolation impossible to ignore.

statements.text: The boycott is dismissed as pointless interference in sport
The boycott is shown to have struck at a deeply valued part of white South African life
The boycott is said to have made isolation impossible to ignore
Mixing politics with sport is called unfair
Both sources judge the boycott the same way

questions.memo: The official (A) calls the boycott pointless meddling; the historian (B) shows it hit hard precisely because sport mattered so much. 'Keep politics out of sport' was itself a way to protect apartheid.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The end of the Cold War helped bring apartheid to the negotiating table.'
questions.thesis: The end of the Cold War helped bring apartheid to the negotiating table.

pool.text: With the USSR gone, South Africa lost its 'anti-communist ally' argument for Western support
The collapse of the communist bloc reduced white fears that liberation meant Soviet domination
It made a negotiated settlement less threatening to the government and its supporters
The Berlin Wall was made of concrete
The USSR was in eastern Europe and Asia
Internal resistance and economic pressure were also pushing toward negotiations

questions.memo: Loss of the anti-communist argument (e1), reduced fear of Soviet domination (e2), and a less threatening settlement (e3) link the Cold War's end to negotiations. e6 is a fair counter — internal pressure mattered too — but the Cold War's end removed a key obstacle.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why the 1973 UN vote was significant.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why the 1973 UN vote was significant.

options.text: It placed the world's moral and legal condemnation of apartheid on record
It made apartheid acceptable internationally
It had no consequences
By declaring apartheid a crime against humanity, the UN gave the anti-apartheid cause legal and moral authority
The vote was held in 1973
The UN has many members
That authority strengthened boycotts, sanctions and solidarity campaigns even though it did not end apartheid at once
Because the vote instantly ended apartheid
Because no one paid attention to the UN

questions.memo: Claim (put condemnation on record) + evidence (declared a crime against humanity, giving legal/moral authority) + explanation (strengthened the pressure campaign) explains its significance.

questions.question: Compare these two views on what brought down apartheid.

source_a.text: Apartheid ended simply because its leaders had a change of heart.

source_b.text: Internal resistance, economic crisis, international isolation and the end of the Cold War together forced the change.

statements.text: Apartheid is said to have ended through a change of heart
Apartheid is shown to have ended through several combined pressures
International isolation and the end of the Cold War are named as factors
The end is explained by leaders simply changing their minds
Both sources explain the end of apartheid the same way

questions.memo: The simple version (A) credits a change of heart; the historian (B) lists many pressures — resistance, economic crisis, isolation, the Cold War's end. Big changes have many causes, not one.

HIS.G12.T2.LIBSTRUG.A1.title: The OAU and the Frontline States
HIS.G12.T2.LIBSTRUG.A1.description: The formation of the Organisation of African Unity (1963, later the AU in 2001), its programme to complete the anti-colonial struggle against white-minority regimes, and the role of the Frontline States in hosting liberation movements and the displaced.
HIS.G12.T2.LIBSTRUG.A1.strand: T2 — Cold War & Anti-colonial Struggles + Liberation Struggles and the OAU
HIS.G12.T2.LIBSTRUG.A1.caps_topic: The Era of the Liberation Struggles and the Politics of Apartheid South Africa on the African Continent
HIS.G12.T2.LIBSTRUG.A1.recovery_strategy: The OAU (1963, later the AU in 2001) was Africa's united front against the remaining white-minority regimes. The Frontline States sheltered liberation movements in exile and the displaced, at real cost to themselves. The struggle was continental, not just internal.

questions.question: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) was founded in:
questions.memo: The OAU was founded in 1963 to unite newly independent African states and continue the anti-colonial struggle.

questions.question: The OAU was renamed the _________ in 2001.
questions.memo: In 2001 the OAU became the African Union (AU). Same body, new name.

questions.question: A main aim of the OAU was to:
options: Complete the anti-colonial struggle against white-minority regimes
questions.expected: Complete the anti-colonial struggle against white-minority regimes
questions.memo: The OAU's programme of action was to finish decolonisation — opposing the white-minority regimes in Rhodesia, the Portuguese colonies and South Africa.

questions.question: True or false: The Frontline States hosted South African and other liberation movements in exile.
questions.memo: The Frontline States — neighbouring independent countries — sheltered liberation movements in exile and supported people displaced by the white-minority regimes.

questions.question: Which body within the OAU coordinated support for liberation movements?
questions.memo: The OAU Liberation Committee coordinated African support for the liberation movements still fighting white-minority rule.

questions.question: True or false: The struggle against apartheid happened only inside South Africa, with no role for other African states.
questions.memo: The struggle was continental: the OAU and the Frontline States supported it from outside South Africa's borders, often at great cost to themselves.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or FALSE about the OAU and Frontline States.

items.text: The OAU was founded in 1963
The OAU supported European colonial powers
The Frontline States hosted liberation movements in exile
The OAU was later renamed the African Union
The Frontline States kept out of the liberation struggle
The OAU aimed to complete decolonisation

questions.memo: True: founded 1963, hosted exiles, renamed the AU, aimed to complete decolonisation. False: supporting colonial powers, staying out of the struggle.

questions.question: Why did hosting liberation movements come at a cost to the Frontline States?
options: Apartheid South Africa attacked and pressured states that sheltered the movements
Hosting them was free of any consequences
The movements paid them large sums
It improved their relations with South Africa
questions.expected: Apartheid South Africa attacked and pressured states that sheltered the movements
questions.memo: Apartheid South Africa raided and destabilised neighbours who hosted liberation movements, so the Frontline States took real economic and military risks to support the struggle.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to describe the OAU.
questions.cloze_template: The [1] was founded in 1963 to unite African states and complete the [2] struggle against white-minority regimes. Its [3] Committee coordinated support for liberation movements. The [4] States hosted exiles, despite attacks from apartheid South Africa. In 2001 the OAU became the [5].
questions.memo: OAU (1963), anti-colonial mission, Liberation Committee, Frontline States, renamed the African Union in 2001.

questions.question: Place these events in chronological order — earliest first.

items.text: Many African colonies become independent (around 1960)
The OAU is founded (1963)
The Frontline States support liberation movements (1970s–80s)
The OAU is renamed the African Union (2001)

questions.memo: Independence (around 1960) → OAU (1963) → Frontline State support (1970s–80s) → African Union (2001).

questions.question: Which white-minority regimes did the OAU's anti-colonial programme target?
options: Those backed by Portugal, Britain and the Republic of South Africa
questions.expected: Those backed by Portugal, Britain and the Republic of South Africa
questions.memo: The OAU targeted the remaining white-minority regimes — the Portuguese colonies, Rhodesia (linked to Britain), and apartheid South Africa.

questions.question: Compare these two views of the OAU's role.

source_a.text: The OAU was a talking shop that achieved nothing for the liberation struggle.

source_b.text: The OAU coordinated diplomatic, material and moral support that sustained liberation movements for decades.

statements.text: The OAU is dismissed as a talking shop that achieved nothing
The OAU is credited with coordinating real support for liberation
The OAU is said to have sustained movements for decades
The OAU is said to have 'achieved nothing'
Both sources judge the OAU the same way

questions.memo: The dismissive account (A) writes the OAU off; the historian (B) credits its diplomatic, material and moral support. Dismissing it as a 'talking shop' ignores the support it actually delivered.

questions.question: What does the existence of the OAU and Frontline States tell us about the anti-apartheid struggle?
options: It was a continental and international effort, not just a South African one
It was fought only by South Africans inside South Africa
It had no support anywhere in Africa
It was led by the apartheid government
questions.expected: It was a continental and international effort, not just a South African one
questions.memo: The OAU and Frontline States show the struggle reached across the continent — many African states and peoples gave support, making it a continental effort.

questions.question: Why did newly independent African states feel a duty to support liberation in southern Africa?
options: They saw the freedom of the continent as incomplete while white-minority regimes remained
They wanted to keep colonialism going
They had no interest in southern Africa
questions.expected: They saw the freedom of the continent as incomplete while white-minority regimes remained
questions.memo: Having won their own independence, many African states believed Africa was not truly free while white-minority regimes survived — so they backed the remaining liberation struggles.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The anti-apartheid struggle was a continental effort, not just a South African one.'
questions.thesis: The anti-apartheid struggle was a continental effort, not just a South African one.

pool.text: The OAU coordinated African support for the liberation movements
The Frontline States hosted exiles and the displaced at real cost to themselves
Independent African states saw the continent's freedom as incomplete while apartheid remained
Africa is a large continent
The OAU had a headquarters
Much of the resistance still took place inside South Africa

questions.memo: OAU coordination (e1), Frontline State support (e2), and shared continental purpose (e3) show a continental effort. e6 is a fair counter — internal resistance was vital — but the struggle also reached across Africa.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining the role of the Frontline States.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining the role of the Frontline States.

options.text: The Frontline States supported liberation movements at real risk to themselves
The Frontline States supported apartheid
The Frontline States played no part in the struggle
They hosted liberation movements in exile and sheltered the displaced, while suffering South African attacks
They were near South Africa
They were independent countries
By bearing these costs, they kept the liberation movements alive and made the struggle a regional one
Because supporting the movements had no consequences
Because they wanted apartheid to continue

questions.memo: Claim (supported at real risk) + evidence (hosted exiles, suffered attacks) + explanation (kept movements alive, made the struggle regional) explains the Frontline States.

questions.question: Compare these two views on the Frontline States.

source_a.text: These neighbouring states meddled recklessly in South Africa's internal affairs.

source_b.text: The Frontline States took great risks to host the movements that the apartheid state was trying to crush.

statements.text: The neighbours are accused of reckless meddling
The neighbours are credited with taking risks to host the movements
The apartheid state is described as trying to crush the movements
The neighbours are said to interfere in 'internal affairs'
Both sources describe the Frontline States the same way

questions.memo: The apartheid view (A) calls them reckless meddlers; the historian (B) recognises their courage and risk. Calling solidarity 'meddling in internal affairs' was a way to delegitimise it.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The OAU made a real contribution to the liberation struggle.'
questions.thesis: The OAU made a real contribution to the liberation struggle.

pool.text: Its Liberation Committee coordinated material and diplomatic support
It kept the liberation of the remaining white-minority regimes on the international agenda
It backed the Frontline States and movements in exile over many years
The OAU was founded in Addis Ababa
Africa has 54 countries today
The OAU was sometimes divided and slow to act

questions.memo: Coordinated support (e1), kept liberation on the agenda (e2), and backed exiles and Frontline States (e3) show a real contribution. e6 is a fair counter — it had weaknesses — but it still helped sustain the struggle.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why the OAU's anti-colonial mission outlasted the first wave of independence.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why the OAU's anti-colonial mission outlasted the first wave of independence.

options.text: White-minority regimes still ruled parts of southern Africa, so the mission continued
All of Africa was free by 1963
The OAU had no anti-colonial mission
Portuguese colonies, Rhodesia and apartheid South Africa remained under white-minority rule after most of Africa was independent
The OAU met regularly
Africa has many languages
Because these regimes survived, the OAU kept supporting liberation movements until they too were free
Because there was nothing left to fight for
Because the OAU supported the white-minority regimes

questions.memo: Claim (regimes still ruled, so the mission went on) + evidence (Portuguese colonies, Rhodesia, apartheid SA remained) + explanation (OAU kept backing liberation until they were free) makes the case.

questions.question: Compare these two views on whether African solidarity mattered to the anti-apartheid struggle.

source_a.text: Apartheid was defeated entirely from within; outside African states made no difference.

source_b.text: Continental solidarity — the OAU, the Frontline States and exile bases — was essential to sustaining the struggle.

statements.text: Apartheid is said to have been defeated entirely from within
Continental solidarity is said to have been essential
The OAU, Frontline States and exile bases are named as important
Outside African states are said to have made no difference
Both sources agree on the role of African solidarity

questions.memo: The inward-looking account (A) credits only internal forces; the historian (B) shows continental solidarity was essential. Both internal and continental effort mattered — ignoring either gives a partial picture.

HIS.G12.T2.LIBSTRUG.A2.title: A continent divided: pro- and anti-liberation states
HIS.G12.T2.LIBSTRUG.A2.description: Why African states did not all support the liberation struggle equally — a comparison of pro-liberation states (Tanzania, Zambia, Nigeria) and anti-liberation states (Malawi, Côte d'Ivoire), and how ideological alignment and economic ties shaped each country's stance.
HIS.G12.T2.LIBSTRUG.A2.strand: T2 — Cold War & Anti-colonial Struggles + Liberation Struggles and the OAU
HIS.G12.T2.LIBSTRUG.A2.caps_topic: The Era of the Liberation Struggles and the Politics of Apartheid South Africa on the African Continent
HIS.G12.T2.LIBSTRUG.A2.recovery_strategy: African support was FRACTURED. Pro-liberation: Tanzania, Zambia, Nigeria. Anti-liberation (kept links with apartheid SA): Malawi, Côte d'Ivoire. The deciding factor was usually ideological alignment and economic ties — countries tied to the West or to South Africa's economy were more reluctant to back the struggle.

questions.question: True or false: All independent African states supported the liberation struggle in South Africa equally.
questions.memo: African support was fractured. Some states strongly backed the liberation movements; others kept economic and diplomatic ties with apartheid South Africa.

questions.question: Which of these was a strong PRO-liberation state?
questions.memo: Tanzania (along with Zambia and Nigeria) strongly supported the liberation movements. Malawi and Côte d'Ivoire were among the anti-liberation states.

questions.question: A country that maintained links with apartheid South Africa rather than backing the liberation struggle was _________.
questions.memo: Malawi (under Banda) and Côte d'Ivoire kept diplomatic and economic links with apartheid South Africa — anti-liberation states.

questions.question: What mainly shaped whether an African state supported the liberation struggle?
options: Its ideological alignment and its economic ties
questions.expected: Its ideological alignment and its economic ties
questions.memo: A country's ideological orientation and its economic links (to the West or to South Africa) largely shaped whether it supported or opposed the liberation movements.

questions.question: True or false: Some African states kept economic ties with apartheid South Africa for their own benefit.
questions.memo: States like Malawi and Côte d'Ivoire valued trade and economic links with South Africa, which made them reluctant to support the liberation struggle.

questions.question: Comparing a pro-liberation state with an anti-liberation state is an example of which historical skill?
questions.memo: Comparing how different states behaved (and why) is comparative analysis — a key skill for understanding the fractured African response.

questions.question: Sort each country by its stance on the liberation struggle.

items.text: Tanzania
Malawi
Zambia
Côte d'Ivoire
Nigeria
A state that kept trade links with Pretoria

questions.memo: Pro-liberation: Tanzania, Zambia, Nigeria. Anti-liberation: Malawi, Côte d'Ivoire (and others that kept ties with Pretoria).

questions.question: Why might an African leader choose to keep ties with apartheid South Africa despite its racism?
options: Economic dependence and ideological alignment could outweigh solidarity
Because they secretly were South African
Because they had no choice in anything
Because the OAU ordered them to
questions.expected: Economic dependence and ideological alignment could outweigh solidarity
questions.memo: Some states depended on South Africa economically or were ideologically aligned with the West, leading them to prioritise their own interests over solidarity with the liberation struggle.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to compare the African states' stances.
questions.cloze_template: African support for the liberation struggle was [1]. States like Tanzania, Zambia and [2] strongly supported it, while [3] and Côte d'Ivoire kept links with apartheid South Africa. A state's [4] alignment and its [5] ties largely decided its stance.
questions.memo: Fractured support: pro (Tanzania, Zambia, Nigeria) vs anti (Malawi, Côte d'Ivoire); ideology and economic ties decided the stance.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show this leader putting economic self-interest above solidarity with the liberation struggle.
questions.source_text: We cannot afford to break with Pretoria; our trade, our jobs and our roads depend on good relations with the south, whatever others may say of their politics.
questions.task: Tap the phrases that reveal economic self-interest over solidarity.

targets.phrase: cannot afford to break with Pretoria
targets.reason: Prioritises ties with apartheid South Africa

targets.phrase: our trade, our jobs and our roads depend on good relations
whatever others may say of their politics
targets.reason: Dismisses the moral objection to apartheid

questions.memo: 'Cannot afford to break with Pretoria', dependence on 'trade, jobs and roads', and brushing aside 'their politics' all show economic interest placed above solidarity.

questions.question: Compare these two African leaders' stances.

source_a.text: Africa cannot be free while our brothers in the south remain in chains; we must support their struggle whatever the cost.

source_b.text: Our duty is to our own people's prosperity; we will trade with whoever benefits us, including South Africa.

statements.text: Solidarity with the liberation struggle is put above cost
Economic benefit is put above solidarity
Trading with South Africa is openly defended
The freedom of 'our brothers in the south' is the priority
Both leaders take the same stance

questions.memo: The pro-liberation leader (A) prioritises solidarity; the anti-liberation leader (B) prioritises economic benefit. The contrast captures exactly why African support was fractured.

questions.question: Why did pro-liberation states support the struggle even at a cost to themselves?
options: They believed Africa's freedom was incomplete while apartheid survived
They were paid by the apartheid government
They had no economy of their own
They wanted to annex South Africa
questions.expected: They believed Africa's freedom was incomplete while apartheid survived
questions.memo: Pro-liberation states like Tanzania and Zambia saw the liberation of southern Africa as part of completing the continent's freedom, and supported it despite the risks and costs.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or a MYTH about the African response to apartheid.

items.text: African states were divided over how to respond to apartheid
Every African state supported the liberation struggle equally
Economic ties influenced some states' stances
No African state ever cooperated with apartheid South Africa
Tanzania and Zambia were strong supporters of liberation
Ideology played no part in shaping states' decisions

questions.memo: True: divided response, economic ties mattered, Tanzania/Zambia pro-liberation. Myths: equal support everywhere, no cooperation with apartheid, ideology irrelevant.

questions.question: What changed the stance of states like Malawi and Côte d'Ivoire over time?
options: The eventual achievement of political freedom in southern Africa altered their position
They were conquered by South Africa
questions.expected: The eventual achievement of political freedom in southern Africa altered their position
questions.memo: As liberation was achieved in the region, the position of formerly anti-liberation states like Malawi and Côte d'Ivoire shifted — the political landscape they had adapted to had changed.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'African support for the liberation struggle was fractured, shaped by interest and ideology.'
questions.thesis: African support for the liberation struggle was fractured, shaped by interest and ideology.

pool.text: States like Tanzania, Zambia and Nigeria backed the struggle strongly
States like Malawi and Côte d'Ivoire kept ties with apartheid South Africa
Economic dependence and ideological alignment shaped each country's choice
Africa has many countries
The OAU had its headquarters in Addis Ababa
Even pro-liberation states sometimes disagreed on tactics

questions.memo: Pro-liberation states (e1), anti-liberation states (e2), and interest/ideology shaping choices (e3) show a fractured response. e6 is a fair counter — even allies differed on tactics — but it reinforces, rather than weakens, the picture of division.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why some African states refused to support the liberation struggle.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why some African states refused to support the liberation struggle.

options.text: Economic dependence and ideological alignment led some states to keep ties with apartheid South Africa
They refused because they admired apartheid's ideals
No state ever refused to support the struggle
States like Malawi and Côte d'Ivoire relied on trade and economic links with South Africa
These states were in Africa
South Africa was a republic
For these governments, their own economic interests and Western alignment outweighed solidarity with the struggle
Because they believed apartheid was just
Because the OAU told them to

questions.memo: Claim (interest and alignment led to ties with apartheid) + evidence (Malawi, Côte d'Ivoire relied on SA trade) + explanation (interests outweighed solidarity) answers the question.

questions.question: Compare these two judgements of states that traded with apartheid South Africa.

source_a.text: They were wise realists who protected their people's livelihoods.

source_b.text: They put short-term economic gain above the freedom of fellow Africans suffering under apartheid.

statements.text: The states are praised as wise realists protecting livelihoods
The states are criticised for putting economic gain above African freedom
Fellow Africans suffering under apartheid are mentioned
The states are described as protecting 'their people's livelihoods'
Both sources judge these states the same way

questions.memo: One view (A) calls them realists; the other (B) calls them self-interested. This is a genuine moral debate about whether solidarity should outweigh national interest.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'A state's economic position helps explain its stance on apartheid.'
questions.thesis: A state's economic position helps explain its stance on apartheid.

pool.text: States economically dependent on South Africa were reluctant to break ties
Landlocked or trade-dependent states relied on South African routes and goods
States less tied to South Africa's economy could more freely support liberation
South Africa is at the southern tip of the continent
Trade involves money
Ideology and leadership also shaped states' choices

questions.memo: Economic dependence (e1), reliance on SA routes/goods (e2), and freedom of less-tied states (e3) link economics to stance. e6 is a fair counter — ideology and leaders mattered too — but economics was a major factor.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why comparing pro- and anti-liberation states is useful.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why comparing pro- and anti-liberation states is useful.

options.text: Comparing them reveals what really shaped African states' decisions
Comparison shows all states were identical
Comparison tells us nothing
Setting Tanzania or Nigeria against Malawi or Côte d'Ivoire highlights the role of ideology and economic ties
These countries are all in Africa
They all have governments
By asking why similar countries behaved differently, we uncover the deeper forces behind their choices
Because comparison hides the real reasons
Because only one country ever mattered

questions.memo: Claim (comparison reveals what shaped decisions) + evidence (pro vs anti highlights ideology and economics) + explanation (asking why similar states differed uncovers deeper forces) explains the value of comparison.

questions.question: Compare these two overall views of the African response to apartheid.

source_a.text: Africa spoke with one united voice against apartheid throughout.

source_b.text: African states were divided: some sacrificed for the struggle while others traded with Pretoria.

statements.text: Africa is said to have spoken with one united voice
African states are shown to have been divided
Some states are said to have traded with Pretoria
The response is described as united 'throughout'
Both sources describe the response the same way

questions.memo: The idealised account (A) imagines a united Africa; the historian (B) shows real division. The 'one united voice' story is more comforting than accurate.

HIS.G12.T2.LIBSTRUG.A3.title: Apartheid's destabilisation of the region and the Harare Declaration
HIS.G12.T2.LIBSTRUG.A3.description: How apartheid South Africa tried to crush the liberation struggle beyond its borders through military and economic destabilisation; the liberation of Namibia and the role of the League of Nations and UN; and the Harare Declaration (1989) setting conditions for a negotiated end to apartheid.
HIS.G12.T2.LIBSTRUG.A3.strand: T2 — Cold War & Anti-colonial Struggles + Liberation Struggles and the OAU
HIS.G12.T2.LIBSTRUG.A3.caps_topic: The Era of the Liberation Struggles and the Politics of Apartheid South Africa on the African Continent
HIS.G12.T2.LIBSTRUG.A3.recovery_strategy: Apartheid South Africa hit BACK across its borders: military raids and economic pressure to destabilise neighbours who sheltered the movements. Namibia's liberation involved the League of Nations and the UN. The Harare Declaration (1989), backed by the OAU, Non-Aligned Movement and UN, set out conditions for negotiations — pointing toward the end of apartheid.

questions.question: How did apartheid South Africa respond to neighbours who supported the liberation struggle?
options: It destabilised them through military raids and economic pressure
It asked the UN to protect them
questions.expected: It destabilised them through military raids and economic pressure
questions.memo: Apartheid South Africa launched raids and applied economic pressure to destabilise neighbours that sheltered liberation movements — making support costly.

questions.question: South West Africa, whose liberation involved the League of Nations and the UN, is today called:
questions.memo: South West Africa became independent as Namibia. Its long road to freedom involved the League of Nations mandate and later the United Nations.

questions.question: The 1989 declaration that set out conditions for a negotiated end to apartheid was the _________ Declaration.
questions.memo: The Harare Declaration (1989), backed by the OAU, the Non-Aligned Movement and the UN, set out conditions for negotiations to end apartheid.

questions.question: True or false: Apartheid South Africa's violence was confined entirely within its own borders.
questions.memo: South Africa attacked and destabilised neighbouring states across the region — its violence reached well beyond its own borders.

questions.question: The Harare Declaration was backed by the OAU, the United Nations and the _________ Movement.
questions.memo: The OAU, the Non-Aligned Movement and the UN together backed the Harare Declaration — giving its conditions for negotiation broad international weight.

questions.question: True or false: The Harare Declaration helped set conditions that shaped the later negotiations to end apartheid.
questions.memo: The Harare Declaration laid out conditions — such as releasing political prisoners and unbanning organisations — that helped frame the negotiations that followed.

questions.question: Sort each item as apartheid AGGRESSION abroad or a STEP TOWARD a settlement.

items.text: Military raids on neighbouring states
The Harare Declaration of 1989
Economic pressure to destabilise neighbours
UN-backed conditions for negotiations
Backing rebel movements against neighbouring governments
International conditions for releasing prisoners and unbanning organisations

questions.memo: Aggression: raids, economic pressure, backing rebels. Settlement: the Harare Declaration and the internationally backed conditions for negotiation.

questions.question: Why did apartheid South Africa try to destabilise its neighbours?
options: To punish them for hosting liberation movements and to weaken the struggle
Because they had attacked South Africa first
questions.expected: To punish them for hosting liberation movements and to weaken the struggle
questions.memo: Destabilisation was meant to punish states that sheltered the movements and to cripple the liberation struggle by attacking its regional bases of support.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to describe apartheid's regional policy and the road to negotiations.
questions.cloze_template: Apartheid South Africa [1] its neighbours through raids and economic pressure to punish them for hosting [2] movements. The freedom of South West Africa, or [3], involved the UN. In 1989 the [4] Declaration, backed by the OAU, UN and Non-Aligned Movement, set [5] for negotiations.
questions.memo: Destabilised neighbours over liberation movements; Namibia's freedom involved the UN; the Harare Declaration (1989) set conditions for negotiations.

questions.question: Place these events in chronological order — earliest first.

items.text: South Africa destabilises neighbouring states (1970s–80s)
The Harare Declaration sets conditions for negotiations (1989)
Namibia becomes independent (1990)
Substantive negotiations to end apartheid begin (early 1990s)

questions.memo: Destabilisation (1970s–80s) → Harare Declaration (1989) → Namibian independence (1990) → negotiations (early 1990s).

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show apartheid South Africa using force to punish a neighbour for supporting the struggle.
questions.source_text: Because that government harbours the terrorists who attack us, our forces have struck their camps across the border and will continue to make the cost of such support unbearable.
questions.task: Tap the phrases that describe cross-border aggression to punish support for the struggle.

targets.phrase: our forces have struck their camps across the border
make the cost of such support unbearable
targets.reason: States the aim of punishing the neighbour for its support

questions.memo: Striking 'camps across the border' to make 'the cost of such support unbearable' is exactly the destabilisation apartheid used against states that backed the liberation struggle. (Note how it labels the movements 'terrorists' to justify the attacks.)

questions.question: Compare these two views of South Africa's regional raids.

source_a.text: These were lawful strikes against terrorist bases threatening our citizens.

source_b.text: These were attacks on neighbouring countries to punish them for sheltering those fighting apartheid.

statements.text: The raids are justified as lawful strikes against terrorists
The raids are described as attacks to punish neighbours
The neighbours are said to be punished for sheltering anti-apartheid fighters
The strikes are called 'lawful' and aimed at 'terrorist bases'
Both sources describe the raids the same way

questions.memo: The government (A) calls the raids lawful anti-terror strikes; the historian (B) sees punishment of neighbours for solidarity. Labelling freedom fighters 'terrorists' was how the raids were justified.

questions.question: Why was the independence of Namibia significant for the wider region?
options: It removed a territory South Africa had controlled and signalled the retreat of white-minority rule
It started the Second World War
questions.expected: It removed a territory South Africa had controlled and signalled the retreat of white-minority rule
questions.memo: Namibia's independence in 1990 ended South African control there and was a clear sign that white-minority rule in the region was coming to an end.

questions.question: What kinds of conditions did the Harare Declaration call for?
options: Steps like releasing political prisoners and unbanning organisations to allow real negotiations
The immediate invasion of South Africa
Cutting off all trade with the whole world
questions.expected: Steps like releasing political prisoners and unbanning organisations to allow real negotiations
questions.memo: The Harare Declaration set out preconditions — such as releasing political prisoners and unbanning organisations — needed for genuine negotiations to take place.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Apartheid South Africa's violence extended far beyond its own borders.'
questions.thesis: Apartheid South Africa's violence extended far beyond its own borders.

pool.text: It launched military raids on neighbouring states
It applied economic pressure to destabilise countries that supported the struggle
It backed rebel movements against neighbouring governments
South Africa is at the southern tip of Africa
South Africa has several neighbours
Most of apartheid's repression still targeted people inside South Africa

questions.memo: Raids (e1), economic pressure (e2), and backing rebels (e3) show violence beyond the borders. e6 is a fair counter — internal repression was vast — but the regional aggression was real and severe.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why apartheid South Africa destabilised its neighbours.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why apartheid South Africa destabilised its neighbours.

options.text: It destabilised neighbours to punish them for supporting the liberation struggle
It destabilised neighbours to help them develop
It never attacked its neighbours
It raided liberation movement bases and pressured states that sheltered exiles
It shared borders with several countries
It had a large army
By making support for the struggle costly, it hoped to isolate the liberation movements and protect itself
Because it wanted its neighbours to prosper
Because its neighbours had invaded it

questions.memo: Claim (punished neighbours for support) + evidence (raided bases, pressured host states) + explanation (made support costly to isolate the movements) explains the destabilisation.

questions.question: Compare these two views of the Harare Declaration.

source_a.text: It was a piece of foreign interference that the South African government rightly ignored.

source_b.text: It set out internationally backed conditions that helped frame the negotiations soon to follow.

statements.text: The declaration is dismissed as foreign interference
The declaration is credited with framing the coming negotiations
The conditions are described as internationally backed
The declaration is said to have been rightly ignored
Both sources judge the declaration the same way

questions.memo: The pro-government view (A) dismisses it; the historian (B) credits it with shaping the negotiations. Calling it 'foreign interference' was a way to resist the conditions it set.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The Harare Declaration helped pave the way for negotiations.'
questions.thesis: The Harare Declaration helped pave the way for negotiations.

pool.text: It set out concrete conditions, like unbanning organisations and releasing prisoners
It had the backing of the OAU, the Non-Aligned Movement and the UN
Its conditions were reflected in the steps taken as negotiations began
It was named after a city
It was issued in 1989
Internal and economic pressures were also pushing toward negotiations

questions.memo: Concrete conditions (e1), broad international backing (e2), and their reflection in the negotiation steps (e3) support the thesis. e6 is a fair counter — other pressures helped too — but the declaration shaped the framework.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why apartheid's destabilisation policy ultimately failed to save it.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why apartheid's destabilisation policy ultimately failed to save it.

options.text: Destabilisation imposed huge costs but could not defeat the struggle or end apartheid's isolation
Destabilisation made apartheid permanently secure
Destabilisation never happened
Despite years of raids and pressure, the liberation movements survived and international condemnation grew
South Africa had a strong army
The region has many countries
Violence abroad could not address the internal injustice or the economic and diplomatic pressures driving change
Because destabilisation was a complete success
Because the movements gave up

questions.memo: Claim (huge costs but could not save apartheid) + evidence (movements survived, condemnation grew) + explanation (violence abroad could not fix internal injustice or external pressure) makes the case.

questions.question: Compare these two judgements of apartheid's regional policy.

source_a.text: By striking hard at its enemies abroad, South Africa kept the region in check and protected itself.

source_b.text: Destabilisation devastated the region but failed to stop the liberation struggle or apartheid's eventual collapse.

statements.text: The policy is judged a success that protected South Africa
The policy is judged to have devastated the region but failed
The eventual collapse of apartheid is mentioned
The policy is said to have 'kept the region in check'
Both sources judge the policy the same way

questions.memo: The pro-government view (A) calls destabilisation a success; the historian (B) shows it devastated the region yet failed to save apartheid. Force abroad inflicted suffering but could not stop the change.

HIS.G12.T3.LEADERS.A1.title: Individuals in history, and P.W. Botha the securocrat
HIS.G12.T3.LEADERS.A1.description: How much individual leaders shape history; P.W. Botha as Defence Minister and his part in the nuclear programme and regional destabilisation; the shift from a 'police state' to a 'military state'; the 1985 State of Emergency and the repression of resistance.
HIS.G12.T3.LEADERS.A1.strand: T3 — The Role of Individual Leaders + Freedom and Democracy / Coming to Terms with the Past
HIS.G12.T3.LEADERS.A1.caps_topic: The Role of Individual Leaders in History during the Apartheid Period
HIS.G12.T3.LEADERS.A1.recovery_strategy: Leaders don't control history at will, but they can be decisive. Botha the SECUROCRAT: as Defence Minister he drove the nuclear programme and regional destabilisation (Angola, 1975); as leader he turned South Africa into a 'military state' and imposed the 1985 State of Emergency, crushing resistance. A 'securocrat' rules through the security forces.

questions.question: Before becoming the country's leader, P.W. Botha served as Minister of:
questions.memo: As Minister of Defence under Vorster, P.W. Botha built up the military and the security establishment that he later relied on as leader.

questions.question: A 'securocrat' is a leader who:
options: Rules mainly through the security forces and military
questions.expected: Rules mainly through the security forces and military
questions.memo: A securocrat governs through the security and military establishment. Botha relied heavily on the army, police and intelligence services.

questions.question: Under Botha, South Africa shifted from a 'police state' toward a _________ state.
questions.memo: Botha moved South Africa from a police state toward a 'military state', with the security establishment dominating government.

questions.question: True or false: Botha imposed a State of Emergency in 1985 to crush popular resistance.
questions.memo: The 1985 State of Emergency gave the security forces sweeping powers to detain, censor and repress as resistance to apartheid surged.

questions.question: According to the CAPS view, individual leaders in history:
options: Cannot change history at will, but can play a decisive role
Have no effect on events at all
questions.expected: Cannot change history at will, but can play a decisive role
questions.memo: The balanced view: leaders cannot bend history to their will, but at key moments they can shape its direction decisively.

questions.question: As Defence Minister, Botha was linked to South Africa's development of _________ weapons and its 1975 invasion of Angola.
questions.memo: Botha was central to South Africa's secret nuclear weapons programme and to the destabilisation of the region, including the 1975 invasion of Angola.

questions.question: Sort each item as part of Botha's role as a SECUROCRAT or NOT part of it.

items.text: Building up the military and security establishment
The 1985 State of Emergency
Destabilising the region militarily
Granting universal adult suffrage
The nuclear weapons programme
Handing power to a democratic parliament

questions.memo: Securocrat: military build-up, State of Emergency, destabilisation, nuclear programme. Not: universal suffrage or democratic hand-over — Botha did the opposite.

questions.question: Why is the question 'what if this individual had acted differently?' useful in history?
options: It helps weigh how much an individual leader actually shaped events
It lets us rewrite the past as we wish
questions.expected: It helps weigh how much an individual leader actually shaped events
questions.memo: Asking how things might have gone otherwise helps historians judge how decisive a particular leader's choices really were.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to describe Botha the securocrat.
questions.cloze_template: As Minister of [1], Botha built up the military and helped develop [2] weapons. As leader he turned South Africa into a '[3] state' run by securocrats and imposed the [4] State of Emergency to crush [5].
questions.memo: Defence Minister → nuclear weapons → 'military state' → 1985 State of Emergency to crush resistance.

questions.question: Place these stages of Botha's career in order — earliest first.

items.text: Botha serves as Minister of Defence under Vorster
South Africa invades Angola (1975)
Botha becomes prime minister (1978)
Botha declares the State of Emergency (1985)

questions.memo: Defence Minister → Angola invasion (1975) → prime minister (1978) → State of Emergency (1985). His rise ran through the security establishment.

questions.question: What did the 1985 State of Emergency allow the security forces to do?
options: Detain people without trial, censor the media and use sweeping powers against protest
Hand power to the liberation movements
questions.expected: Detain people without trial, censor the media and use sweeping powers against protest
questions.memo: The State of Emergency gave the security forces vast powers — detention without trial, censorship, and the suppression of protest — to try to crush the rising resistance.

questions.question: Compare these two views of P.W. Botha's leadership style.

source_a.text: President Botha is a strong, decisive leader who keeps order in dangerous times.

source_b.text: Botha ruled through the security forces, detaining thousands and crushing dissent under emergency powers.

statements.text: Botha is praised as a strong leader keeping order
Botha is described as ruling through the security forces and crushing dissent
Thousands of detentions under emergency powers are mentioned
Botha is described as keeping order 'in dangerous times'
Both sources describe Botha's rule the same way

questions.memo: The pro-government paper (A) praises Botha's 'strength'; the historian (B) describes repression and mass detention. 'Keeping order' was the government's name for crushing dissent.

questions.question: Why did Botha rely so heavily on the military and security forces?
options: He believed force could contain the rising resistance and protect apartheid
He had no army to use
questions.expected: He believed force could contain the rising resistance and protect apartheid
questions.memo: Facing mounting resistance, Botha trusted the security establishment to hold the line for apartheid — making him the classic securocrat.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or a MYTH about Botha as a securocrat.

items.text: Botha built up the security and military establishment
Botha relied on democratic debate rather than force
Botha imposed a State of Emergency in 1985
Botha had no role in regional destabilisation
South Africa developed nuclear weapons in this era
Botha was a leader of the liberation movements

questions.memo: True: built up security forces, 1985 Emergency, nuclear weapons. Myths: ruled by debate, no role in destabilisation, leader of the liberation movements.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'P.W. Botha governed as a securocrat.'
questions.thesis: P.W. Botha governed as a securocrat.

pool.text: He built up and relied on the military and security establishment
He imposed the 1985 State of Emergency, giving the security forces sweeping powers
He used the military to destabilise the region and crush internal resistance
Botha was born in the Orange Free State
Botha had a long political career
He also introduced some political reforms

questions.memo: Reliance on the security establishment (e1), the State of Emergency (e2), and military repression (e3) define the securocrat. e6 is a fair counter — he did reform — which is exactly the 'reformer or securocrat' debate.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining the balanced view of individuals in history.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining the balanced view of individuals in history.

options.text: Individuals cannot bend history at will, but they can shape it at key moments
Individuals control history completely
Individuals never affect history
Botha worked within broad forces, yet his choices on emergency rule and reform decisively shaped events
Botha was a politician
South Africa is a country
Asking what might have happened had he acted differently shows both the limits and the real power of individual leaders
Because leaders are the only cause of events
Because leaders are irrelevant

questions.memo: Claim (not at will, but decisive at moments) + evidence (Botha worked within forces yet shaped events) + explanation (the 'what if' question shows both limits and power) gives the balanced view.

questions.question: Compare these two views on the State of Emergency.

source_a.text: The emergency measures were a regrettable necessity to restore calm and protect citizens.

source_b.text: The State of Emergency unleashed mass detentions, censorship and police violence against those resisting apartheid.

statements.text: The emergency is justified as a regrettable necessity to restore calm
The emergency is described as unleashing detentions and police violence
Censorship is named as part of the emergency
The measures are presented as protecting citizens
Both sources describe the emergency the same way

questions.memo: The government (A) calls the emergency a regrettable necessity; the historian (B) records mass detention, censorship and violence. 'Restoring calm' meant crushing resistance.
